power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .057", "p = .13"), Sentence = c("TAAR5 A nonsignificant increase in methylation was observed in BPD compared with controls, with consistent direction across array analysis (p = .057) and pyrosequencing (p = .13).", "TAAR5 A nonsignificant increase in methylation was observed in BPD compared with controls, with consistent direction across array analysis (p = .057) and pyrosequencing (p = .13)." )), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

info.title: Before Borderline Personality Disorder: A Narrative Review of Etiology and Developmental Integration

text.text: Background: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) is a prevalent and highly impairing condition whose origins cannot be explained by a single causal pathway.
Contemporary research and theory inform a developmental view in which genetic, neurobiological, epigenetic, environmental, and psychological factors may interact recursively across time.
Summary: This narrative review synthesizes evidence and theoretical perspectives on the origins of BPD across biological, epigenetic, environmental, social, psychological, and psychodynamic domains.
Genetic and neurobiological findings point to polygenic vulnerability, heterogeneous frontolimbic alterations, altered stress-response systems, and possible inflammatory and oxidative mechanisms.
Epigenetic research examines possible biological embedding of adversity in stressregulation, neuroplasticity, and neurotransmission pathways.
Environmental evidence highlights associations with childhood adversity, invalidating caregiving, parental psychopathology, peer victimization, socioeconomic disadvantage, and cultural context.

Psychological and psychodynamic models propose how temperament, maladaptive schemas, attachment disruption, emotion dysregulation, impaired mentalization, and fragmented self-other representations contribute to borderline pathology.
Evidence is stronger for associations than for the causal sequences connecting these domains, and BPD specificity remains incompletely established.

The review brings these accounts into a developmental synthesis, examining their convergence and differences and tracing proposed reciprocal relationships among biological vulnerability, caregiving and broader environments, psychological capacities, and subjective experience from infancy through adolescence.
Messages: BPD can be understood within a framework of multiple interacting developmental pathways rather than a single cause.

Equifinality, multifinality, and differential susceptibility provide perspectives on why different individuals may arrive at similar borderline presentations through distinct routes, while similar risk factors may lead to divergent outcomes.

The synthesis translates these relationships into testable propositions about developmental sequences, reciprocal influences, protective processes, and what distinguishes borderline trajectories from other outcomes.
It also informs individualized clinical formulation by connecting developmental vulnerabilities with current difficulties and available supports.
equifinality, multifinality, and differential susceptibility [12,16]  have been considered in relation to BPD [13,15,17,18].

We consider these principles alongside transactional [19]  and bioecological [20]    perspectives, distinguishing theoretical propositions from empirical findings, evaluating the strength and specificity of the evidence, and formulating testable developmental propositions.

This article is a clinically oriented narrative synthesis informed by searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Google Scholar, and Web of Science through October 2026, supplemented by backward and forward citation searching.
Searches and source selection were iterative and guided by the review's clinical and theoretical aims, rather than by a prespecified search strategy or formal eligibility criteria.
Sources were selected for their relevance to BPD etiology and the developmental and theoretical perspectives considered.
Selection and interpretation involved author judgement, with evidence weighted according to methodological quality, temporal ordering, replication, consistency, and comparison groups.
Systematic reviews and meta-analyses were considered alongside primary studies and their limitations; theoretical works informed proposed mechanisms rather than providing empirical confirmation.

This section integrates existing perspectives on BPD's etiology: we examine how biological dispositions, environmental experiences, and developing psychological capacities may influence one another, identifying convergence, complementarity, and disagreement among theories.

This integration considers proposed relationships concerning how patterns of functioning form, become activated, persist, and change, while distinguishing theoretical propositions from empirical findings.
The accounts concern different constructs and outcomes (borderline features, categorical BPD, and broader personality dysfunction or organization), which require separate consideration.

Our aim is to connect these theoretical perspectives across developmental periods and levels of functioning and identify their implications for the subsequent critical examination of available evidence.

Sameroff's transactional model provides a foundation for the approach outlined above by conceptualizing development as a dynamic process in which individuals and their environments change both through their own developmental processes and through reciprocal influences [19,21,22].

Borderline Personality Disorder (BPD) has an estimated point prevalence of about 1.6% and a lifetime prevalence of up to 5.9%, and is diagnosed similarly in men and in women in the general population (in the United States of America) but approximately three times more often in women than in men in clinical settings [1] [2] [3].

text.text: BPD is increasingly understood not simply through a diathesis-stress lens, but through developmental frameworks proposing reciprocal influences among biological, epigenetic, psychological, and environmental factors.

In this view, outcomes may reflect not only vulnerability under adversity but also plasticity, whereby the same susceptibilities may contribute to pathology or resilience depending on context [12] [13] [14] [15].
text.formatted: In this view, outcomes may reflect not only vulnerability under adversity but also plasticity, whereby the same susceptibilities may contribute to pathology or resilience depending on context <ref type="bibr">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[13]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[15]</ref>.

text.text: How these factors work together over time, and why shared vulnerabilities contribute to BPD rather than another disorder or sustained adaptation, remain incompletely understood.

In this paper, we explore the biological, epigenetic, environmental, and psychological dimensions of BPD, and critically integrate existing perspectives across psychiatry, neuroscience, and psychotherapy to examine its possible developmental pathways.
The principles of through bidirectional exchanges, both individuals and their environments are modified, thereby changing subsequent development.

His unified theory of development integrates four complementary perspectives: personal change, concerning the development and reorganization of individual capacities; context, encompassing interpersonal relationships and broader ecological environments; regulation, emphasizing the interdependence of self-and other-regulation; and representation, addressing how experiences become organized into meanings and expectations that influence subsequent functioning [21, 22].
text.formatted: His unified theory of development integrates four complementary perspectives: personal change, concerning the development and reorganization of individual capacities; context, encompassing interpersonal relationships and broader ecological environments; regulation, emphasizing the interdependence of self-and other-regulation; and representation, addressing how experiences become organized into meanings and expectations that influence subsequent functioning <ref type="bibr">[21,</ref> <ref type="bibr">22]</ref>.

text.text: Together, Sameroff's four perspectives offer a framework for examining how different BPD theories emphasize individual development, environmental contexts, regulatory processes, and psychological representations, without assuming that their proposed mechanisms are equivalent [19].
text.formatted: Together, Sameroff's four perspectives offer a framework for examining how different BPD theories emphasize individual development, environmental contexts, regulatory processes, and psychological representations, without assuming that their proposed mechanisms are equivalent <ref type="bibr">[19]</ref>.

text.text: Building on earlier transactional and developmental perspectives, Judd and McGlashan [23] proposed that adverse environments and neurobehavioral vulnerabilities may contribute to disturbances in attachment and information processing, potentially impairing the integration of cognitive, emotional, and behavioral capacities and contributing to identity disturbance and relational instability.
text.formatted: Building on earlier transactional and developmental perspectives, Judd and McGlashan <ref type="bibr">[23]</ref> proposed that adverse environments and neurobehavioral vulnerabilities may contribute to disturbances in attachment and information processing, potentially impairing the integration of cognitive, emotional, and behavioral capacities and contributing to identity disturbance and relational instability.

text.text: Drawing on longitudinal and observational evidence, Lyons-Ruth and Brumariu [24] proposed a tentative developmental cascade model for BPD in which disruptions in the development of age specific competencies may contribute to further difficulties at subsequent developmental stages.
text.formatted: Drawing on longitudinal and observational evidence, Lyons-Ruth and Brumariu <ref type="bibr">[24]</ref> proposed a tentative developmental cascade model for BPD in which disruptions in the development of age specific competencies may contribute to further difficulties at subsequent developmental stages.

text.text: The models emphasize different aspects: Judd and McGlashan foreground the integration of multiple developmental capacities, whereas Lyons-Ruth and Brumariu focus on how difficulties may extend across successive developmental periods.

Of particular relevance to diagnostic specificity, Lyons-Ruth and Brumariu contrast proposed trajectories toward BPD characterized by continued relationship-seeking and sensitivity to caregiver withdrawal with pathways toward antisocial behavior characterized by more coercive interactions and aggression.
However, the proposed distinctions remain provisional.
Bronfenbrenner and Morris's [20] bioecological model complements Sameroff's transactional perspective by specifying the conditions under which recurring interactions contribute to development.
text.formatted: Bronfenbrenner and Morris's <ref type="bibr">[20]</ref> bioecological model complements Sameroff's transactional perspective by specifying the conditions under which recurring interactions contribute to development.

text.text: The Process-Person-Context-Time (PPCT) model defines proximal processes as progressively more complex, reciprocal interactions of the individual with people, objects, and symbols that take place regularly over extended periods.
The effects depend on the person, immediate and broader contexts, and time.
Navarro et al. [25] elaborated the concept of inverse proximal processes through which recurring interactions may contribute to maladaptive development.
text.formatted: Navarro et al. <ref type="bibr">[25]</ref> elaborated the concept of inverse proximal processes through which recurring interactions may contribute to maladaptive development.

text.text: Sameroff [21, 22] situates changing self-and other-regulation within a biopsychosocial system encompassing neurophysiological, neuroendocrine, genomic, and epigenomic processes.
text.formatted: Sameroff <ref type="bibr">[21,</ref> <ref type="bibr">22]</ref> situates changing self-and other-regulation within a biopsychosocial system encompassing neurophysiological, neuroendocrine, genomic, and epigenomic processes.

text.text: McLaughlin and Gabard-Durnam [26] further distinguish experience-expectant learning -during sensitive periods -from experience-dependent learning throughout life, although plasticity varies with age and experience.
text.formatted: McLaughlin and Gabard-Durnam <ref type="bibr">[26]</ref> further distinguish experience-expectant learning -during sensitive periods -from experience-dependent learning throughout life, although plasticity varies with age and experience.

text.text: Taken together, these accounts suggest how the nature, timing, and duration of experiences may shape psychological capacities and biological functioning, which may, in turn, further influence transactions.
They provide a framework for biological embedding, rather than evidence of particular biological causal pathways or sensitive periods specific to BPD.
Psychoanalytic theorists have addressed early relational development through the proposed formation of psychological capacities within caregiving relationships.

Winnicott [27] proposed that a reliable and developmentally responsive holding environment supports ego integration and continuity of being as the infant progresses from absolute dependence through relative dependence toward greater independence.
text.formatted: Winnicott <ref type="bibr">[27]</ref> proposed that a reliable and developmentally responsive holding environment supports ego integration and continuity of being as the infant progresses from absolute dependence through relative dependence toward greater independence.

text.text: Bion [28] developed the concepts of maternal reverie, containment, and alphafunction to describe how emotional experiences may be processed within the caregiver-infant relationship, with functions initially provided by the caregiver potentially becoming part of the child's developing capacity for thinking.
text.formatted: Bion <ref type="bibr">[28]</ref> developed the concepts of maternal reverie, containment, and alphafunction to describe how emotional experiences may be processed within the caregiver-infant relationship, with functions initially provided by the caregiver potentially becoming part of the child's developing capacity for thinking.

text.text: Drawing on quantitative observational research on mother-infant interactions and psychoanalytic theory, Beebe and Lachmann [29] distinguish self-contingency (the predictability of an individual's own behavioral rhythms) from interactive contingency (the coordination of behavior with a partner), describing their interdependence and contribution to procedural expectancies.
text.formatted: Drawing on quantitative observational research on mother-infant interactions and psychoanalytic theory, Beebe and Lachmann <ref type="bibr">[29]</ref> distinguish self-contingency (the predictability of an individual's own behavioral rhythms) from interactive contingency (the coordination of behavior with a partner), describing their interdependence and contribution to procedural expectancies.

text.text: Self-contingency is a narrower construct than self-regulation and should not be equated with it.
Considered together, these approaches raise the question of how patterned exchanges relate to developing capacities to organize emotional experience.
In our integration, capacities shaped through earlier relationships may subsequently influence participation in later ones.

Considered through Sameroff's general transactional framework, Linehan's [30] biosocial theory can be understood as an account of how individual emotional vulnerability and invalidating environmental responses may become interconnected across development and potentially contribute to BPD.
text.formatted: Considered through Sameroff's general transactional framework, Linehan's <ref type="bibr">[30]</ref> biosocial theory can be understood as an account of how individual emotional vulnerability and invalidating environmental responses may become interconnected across development and potentially contribute to BPD.

text.text: Heightened emotional sensitivity and reactivity, together with slower recovery from arousal, may interact with invalidating environmental responses, potentially hindering the development of effective emotion regulation.

Crowell et al. [13] further propose that in a substantial subset of individuals who later develop BPD, early trait impulsivity may precede heightened emotional sensitivity and emerge independently of emotion dysregulation, potentially influencing caregiver responses and subsequent emotional and behavioral development.
text.formatted: Crowell et al. <ref type="bibr">[13]</ref> further propose that in a substantial subset of individuals who later develop BPD, early trait impulsivity may precede heightened emotional sensitivity and emerge independently of emotion dysregulation, potentially influencing caregiver responses and subsequent emotional and behavioral development.

text.text: While Linehan emphasizes emotion dysregulation as central to BPD, Judd and McGlashan situate it within a broader disturbance involving attachment organization and the integration of cognitive, emotional, and behavioral capacities.

A three-wave longitudinal observational study found partial support for Linehan's biosocial propositions, including reciprocal prospective associations between emotion dysregulation and borderline features and an association between parental invalidation and subsequent emotion dysregulation.

However, within-person reciprocal associations between emotional vulnerability and parental invalidation were not consistent across assessment intervals, and parental invalidation did not independently predict borderline features six months later after adjustment for baseline features [31].
text.formatted: However, within-person reciprocal associations between emotional vulnerability and parental invalidation were not consistent across assessment intervals, and parental invalidation did not independently predict borderline features six months later after adjustment for baseline features <ref type="bibr">[31]</ref>.

text.text: Crowell et al. [13] also identify overlapping vulnerabilities implicated in ADHD, conduct disorder, substance use disorders, and antisocial pathology, leaving unresolved which developmental conditions differentiate borderline outcomes from other forms of psychopathology.
text.formatted: Crowell et al. <ref type="bibr">[13]</ref> also identify overlapping vulnerabilities implicated in ADHD, conduct disorder, substance use disorders, and antisocial pathology, leaving unresolved which developmental conditions differentiate borderline outcomes from other forms of psychopathology.

text.text: Fruzzetti et al. [32] further propose that recurring family transactions may shape not only emotion regulation but also how children evaluate the validity of their own emotional experience.
text.formatted: Fruzzetti et al. <ref type="bibr">[32]</ref> further propose that recurring family transactions may shape not only emotion regulation but also how children evaluate the validity of their own emotional experience.

text.text: Repeated dismissal or misinterpretation of distress may interfere with learning to identify, label, tolerate, and communicate emotions, while inhibition or escalation of distress may elicit further invalidation or responses that inadvertently reinforce these patterns.
Over time, these exchanges may contribute to self-invalidation, diminishing trust in one's own emotional experience, while also shaping expectations concerning others' responsiveness.

On the other hand, responses that validate the child's emotional experience may facilitate more adaptive communication and emotional understanding, potentially contributing to changes in subsequent family interactions.

Thus, a proposed developmental process may be connected to a possible maintenance process: responses to emotions may shape self-evaluation, which may subsequently influence emotional communication and others' responses.
However, the progression from invalidation to self-invalidation remains insufficiently tested prospectively.
Importantly, Fruzzetti et al.'s transactional model does not assign causal responsibility or blame exclusively to caregivers.
Apart from their influence on emotion regulation, recurring caregiver-child interactions may also shape expectations concerning the availability and responsiveness of others.
Bowlby's [33] attachment theory conceptualizes these expectations as internal working models that influence subsequent interpersonal experiences and behavior.
text.formatted: Bowlby's <ref type="bibr">[33]</ref> attachment theory conceptualizes these expectations as internal working models that influence subsequent interpersonal experiences and behavior.

text.text: Gunderson [34] proposed intolerance of aloneness as a core difficulty in BPD, linking it to alternating patterns of anxious proximity-seeking and defensive detachment, as well as impaired object constancy -the difficulty maintaining reassuring internal representations of others in their absence.
text.formatted: Gunderson <ref type="bibr">[34]</ref> proposed intolerance of aloneness as a core difficulty in BPD, linking it to alternating patterns of anxious proximity-seeking and defensive detachment, as well as impaired object constancy -the difficulty maintaining reassuring internal representations of others in their absence.

text.text: In a narrative review of 13 empirical studies, Agrawal et al. [35] identified associations between BPD and unresolved, preoccupied, and fearful adult attachment patterns, while noting methodological heterogeneity and partial diagnostic circularity arising from BPD's interpersonal diagnostic criteria.
text.formatted: In a narrative review of 13 empirical studies, Agrawal et al. <ref type="bibr">[35]</ref> identified associations between BPD and unresolved, preoccupied, and fearful adult attachment patterns, while noting methodological heterogeneity and partial diagnostic circularity arising from BPD's interpersonal diagnostic criteria.

text.text: In a theoretical review, Gunderson et al. [36] discussed interpersonal hypersensitivity, emotional dysregulation, failed mentalization, and excess aggression as competing explanations of BPD's core psychopathology, highlighting differences in their proposed primary mechanisms and explanatory scope.
text.formatted: In a theoretical review, Gunderson et al. <ref type="bibr">[36]</ref> discussed interpersonal hypersensitivity, emotional dysregulation, failed mentalization, and excess aggression as competing explanations of BPD's core psychopathology, highlighting differences in their proposed primary mechanisms and explanatory scope.

text.text: Gunderson's interpersonal hypersensitivity formulation does not treat emotion dysregulation, failed mentalization, or excess aggression as the primary explanatory mechanisms, instead emphasizing relational sensitivity.
However, the relative explanatory primacy of these accounts remains unresolved.
Attachment relationships may shape not only expectations of others but also the capacity to understand behavior in terms of underlying mental states.

Fonagy and Luyten [37] propose that caregivers' recognition and contingent, marked mirroring of a child's emotional experiences contribute to the development of mentalization and affect regulation, while disruptions in these processes may compromise the differentiation of mental states of self and other.
text.formatted: Fonagy and Luyten <ref type="bibr">[37]</ref> propose that caregivers' recognition and contingent, marked mirroring of a child's emotional experiences contribute to the development of mentalization and affect regulation, while disruptions in these processes may compromise the differentiation of mental states of self and other.

text.text: Applied to BPD, a relatively low threshold for attachment-system activation may lead to heightened arousal and deactivation of explicit (controlled) mentalization, increasing reliance on implicit (automatic) processing and potentially distorting interpretations of others' intentions.
This formulation emphasizes context-dependent difficulties in mentalization.

In a meta-analysis comparing individuals with BPD with healthy controls, Németh et al. [38] found evidence of difficulties in mental-state reasoning and cognitive theory of mind (ToM), but not consistently in mental-state decoding, while affective findings varied by task.
text.formatted: In a meta-analysis comparing individuals with BPD with healthy controls, Németh et al. <ref type="bibr">[38]</ref> found evidence of difficulties in mental-state reasoning and cognitive theory of mind (ToM), but not consistently in mental-state decoding, while affective findings varied by task.

text.text: These largely cross-sectional comparisons do not directly test Fonagy and Luyten's proposed developmental mechanisms.

Considered alongside biosocial and attachment perspectives, the mentalization-based formulation suggests a possible developmental pathway in which relationships sought for reassurance and emotional regulation may also become contexts in which heightened arousal interferes with the capacity to understand and navigate interpersonal experiences.
This remains an integrative hypothesis concerning some developmental trajectories toward BPD.

Whereas mentalization-based theories underline issues in understanding mental states, Kernberg's [39] formulation of borderline personality organization, based on object-relations theory and ego psychology, addresses the structural organization and integration of affectively charged selfand object representations.
text.formatted: Whereas mentalization-based theories underline issues in understanding mental states, Kernberg's <ref type="bibr">[39]</ref> formulation of borderline personality organization, based on object-relations theory and ego psychology, addresses the structural organization and integration of affectively charged selfand object representations.

text.text: In his formulation, splitting and related primitive defensive operations, such as primitive idealization and devaluation, support the separation of contradictory positive and negative self-and object representations, contributing to identity diffusion and unstable interpersonal relationships.

Importantly, Kernberg's borderline personality organization involves generally preserved self-other boundaries and reality testing despite identity diffusion, although reality testing may become transiently impaired under severe stress.
Kernberg's concept of borderline personality organization refers to a broader psychodynamic level of personality functioning rather than a specific diagnostic category.
However, Kernberg also explicitly recognized and discussed BPD as a clinical syndrome.

Alongside Fonagy and Luyten's mentalization-based model, Kernberg's theory places explanatory emphasis on the integration of representations, rather than primarily on the capacity to interpret mental states under attachment-related arousal.

A possible connection is that difficulties holding conflicting experiences of a person together may constrain interpretations during conflict, while recurrent disruptions in understanding may hinder the revision of representations.
These directions require separate examination; their reciprocity remains hypothetical.

Cognitive and schema models propose that enduring beliefs shape the interpretation of interpersonal events and coping responses [40, 41] describe early maladaptive schemas and the coping responses associated with their activation.
text.formatted: Cognitive and schema models propose that enduring beliefs shape the interpretation of interpersonal events and coping responses <ref type="bibr">[40,</ref> <ref type="bibr">41]</ref> describe early maladaptive schemas and the coping responses associated with their activation.

text.text: For example, in BPD, schemas involving mistrust, abandonment, or defectiveness may shape the interpretation of ambiguous situations, such as a delayed response from a significant other, as rejection, particularly during heightened emotional arousal.
Reassurance seeking, withdrawal, or anger may, in turn, influence others' responses, potentially reinforcing the initial expectations and maintaining these patterns.
This illustrates both activation and possible maintenance; however, the initial formation of these patterns requires a separate developmental explanation.
Young et al. [41] additionally describe shifts between schema modes, conceptualized as temporarily activated configurations of schemas, emotional states, and coping responses.
text.formatted: Young et al. <ref type="bibr">[41]</ref> additionally describe shifts between schema modes, conceptualized as temporarily activated configurations of schemas, emotional states, and coping responses.

text.text: Within our synthesis, persistence may reside partly in recurring patterns of change in emotion, interpretation, and behavior, despite substantial variation in functioning across situations.
Whether these patterns generalize to new contexts or reflect continuing adverse conditions is an empirical question.
These theories help clarify how experiences acquire meaning.

In our integration, subjective experience denotes the evolving organization of bodily and affective states, expectations, and interpretations, rather than an additional etiological factor alongside biology and environment.

Selfinvalidation concerns whether one's emotional response is considered legitimate [32]; mentalization concerns how mental states are understood [37]; and cognitive and schema formulations concern how prior beliefs guide appraisal [40, 41].
text.formatted: Selfinvalidation concerns whether one's emotional response is considered legitimate <ref type="bibr">[32]</ref>; mentalization concerns how mental states are understood <ref type="bibr">[37]</ref>; and cognitive and schema formulations concern how prior beliefs guide appraisal <ref type="bibr">[40,</ref> <ref type="bibr">41]</ref>.

text.text: Thus, similar interpersonal events may be understood and responded to differently.

Baptista et al. [42] add a related consideration through the sense of agencythe experience of control over one's actions and their consequences -distinguishing interrelated implicit (pre-reflective) and explicit (reflective) aspects.
text.formatted: Baptista et al. <ref type="bibr">[42]</ref> add a related consideration through the sense of agencythe experience of control over one's actions and their consequences -distinguishing interrelated implicit (pre-reflective) and explicit (reflective) aspects.

text.text: In this synthesis, attention is given to how individuals experience their own actions and their effects, alongside how they interpret events and emotions.
Attention to subjective meaning complements consideration of objective adversity.
Cicchetti and Rogosch's [16] principles of equifinality and multifinality situate these proposed processes within developmental heterogeneity.
text.formatted: Cicchetti and Rogosch's <ref type="bibr">[16]</ref> principles of equifinality and multifinality situate these proposed processes within developmental heterogeneity.

text.text: Equifinality describes different pathways leading to similar outcomes; multifinality describes similar initial conditions leading to different outcomes within differently organized developmental systems.

Applied to BPD, these principles allow for different configurations and sequences of dispositions, relational experiences, and psychological capacities, while recognizing that shared vulnerabilities may also accompany other psychopathology or adaptive functioning.

Beauchaine et al. [43], for example, proposed a model in which biology, sex, and environment interact, and in which partially shared vulnerabilities, such as trait impulsivity, may contribute to divergent antisocial and borderline outcomes, with sex-related biological and environmental influences hypothesized to differentiate these trajectories.
text.formatted: Beauchaine et al. <ref type="bibr">[43]</ref>, for example, proposed a model in which biology, sex, and environment interact, and in which partially shared vulnerabilities, such as trait impulsivity, may contribute to divergent antisocial and borderline outcomes, with sex-related biological and environmental influences hypothesized to differentiate these trajectories.

text.text: Whereas Lyons-Ruth and Brumariu [24] emphasize the possible sequence of developmental difficulties, Beauchaine et al. focus on how partly shared liabilities might lead to different outcomes.
text.formatted: Whereas Lyons-Ruth and Brumariu <ref type="bibr">[24]</ref> emphasize the possible sequence of developmental difficulties, Beauchaine et al. focus on how partly shared liabilities might lead to different outcomes.

text.text: Equifinality and multifinality describe these possibilities without identifying their mechanisms.

Our integration therefore locates a question of specificity in the relationships among shared processes: whether particular configurations and sequences help explain borderline outcomes beyond the separate contributions of their components.

While equifinality and multifinality describe the possibility of convergent and divergent developmental outcomes, differential susceptibility offers a complementary perspective on why environmental influences may have different consequences across individuals.
Going beyond the diathesis-stress model, Belsky and Pluess [12] proposed that some individuals may be more responsive both to adverse and supportive environmental conditions.
text.formatted: Going beyond the diathesis-stress model, Belsky and Pluess <ref type="bibr">[12]</ref> proposed that some individuals may be more responsive both to adverse and supportive environmental conditions.

text.text: Heightened sensitivity to adversity or a statistical individual-environment interaction alone does not establish differential susceptibility; the model specifically requires greater responsiveness to both unfavorable and favorable environments [44].
text.formatted: Heightened sensitivity to adversity or a statistical individual-environment interaction alone does not establish differential susceptibility; the model specifically requires greater responsiveness to both unfavorable and favorable environments <ref type="bibr">[44]</ref>.

text.text: Applying this general framework to BPD, Rioux et al. [15] proposed that temperamental characteristics implicated in theories of BPD, including emotional reactivity and impulsivity, might indicate differences in environmental plasticity rather than acting exclusively as fixed risk factors.
text.formatted: Applying this general framework to BPD, Rioux et al. <ref type="bibr">[15]</ref> proposed that temperamental characteristics implicated in theories of BPD, including emotional reactivity and impulsivity, might indicate differences in environmental plasticity rather than acting exclusively as fixed risk factors.

text.text: Importantly, temperamental sensitivity should not be used interchangeably with emotion dysregulation.

Unlike transactional models, differential susceptibility concerns variation in responsiveness to environmental conditions rather than specifying the reciprocal processes through which individuals and contexts change.
Within our integration, it suggests a possible moderating role for individual dispositions in the influence of relational environments on developing regulatory and representational capacities.
Direct evidence that BPD-related characteristics predict greater responsiveness to both adverse and supportive environments remains limited.
Whereas differential susceptibility concerns individual differences in environmental responsiveness, resilience concerns the maintenance or recovery of mental health despite adversity.

Kalisch et al.'s [45] positive appraisal style theory of resilience (PASTOR) distinguishes this outcome from its proposed mechanisms, including positive situation classification, reappraisal, and interference inhibition.
text.formatted: Kalisch et al.'s <ref type="bibr">[45]</ref> positive appraisal style theory of resilience (PASTOR) distinguishes this outcome from its proposed mechanisms, including positive situation classification, reappraisal, and interference inhibition.

text.text: Social support may reduce adversity, buffer its effects, or influence appraisal; these are distinct possibilities.

Fonagy et al. [46, 47] connect resilience with mentalization and epistemic trust: understanding behavior in terms of mental states may support appraisal, while openness to personally relevant, generalizable social communication may allow established interpretations to be revised.
text.formatted: Fonagy et al. <ref type="bibr">[46,</ref> <ref type="bibr">47]</ref> connect resilience with mentalization and epistemic trust: understanding behavior in terms of mental states may support appraisal, while openness to personally relevant, generalizable social communication may allow established interpretations to be revised.

text.text: These capacities are related in their conceptual account but are not interchangeable.
Epistemic mistrust may initially be adaptive in adverse childhood environments, but its persistence may restrict learning and adaptation when those circumstances change.
Seen through Sameroff's regulation and representation perspectives, these accounts distinguish opportunities for support from the capacities through which support may be used.
In our synthesis, changes in either of them may have far reaching consequences for better or worse, potentially reinforcing or modifying established patterns.
Such opportunities extend beyond caregiving to other, wider social settings [20].
text.formatted: Such opportunities extend beyond caregiving to other, wider social settings <ref type="bibr">[20]</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, difficulties may not originate as useful adaptations, and their persistence may reflect continuing adversity as well as established expectations or responses.
These accounts therefore connect opportunities for adaptive change with both individual functioning and actual environmental conditions.
The timing, duration, and order of these relationships are also significant.
Whereas transactions refer to reciprocal person-environment changes, developmental cascades concern how functioning in one period may influence competencies and traits in later periods [24].
text.formatted: Whereas transactions refer to reciprocal person-environment changes, developmental cascades concern how functioning in one period may influence competencies and traits in later periods <ref type="bibr">[24]</ref>.

text.text: Early caregiving may be particularly relevant to emerging co-regulation and relational expectations; peer relationships, increasingly complex mentalization, and identity formation play a significant role later on.
Such shifts do not establish BPD-specific sensitive periods, nor should timing lead us to ignore exposure duration or cumulative adversity.
In our integration, earlier patterns of functioning may also shape how subsequent challenges are interpreted and negotiated, apart from contributing through accumulated risk.
A process may therefore change its developmental function: a response that facilitates adaptation under one set of demands may restrict functioning under another.
However, the complete cascade proposed for BPD remains unvalidated, and whether more than one such cascade exists is a topic for empirical study.
This distinguishes the formation of a pattern from its situational activation, persistence, and modification.
These are separate explanatory questions, not universal developmental stages; a process contributing to initial formation need not be the process that later sustains it.
The developmental outcome under consideration also depends on how borderline pathology is defined.

In the categorical Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR) classification, BPD is diagnosed through a specified combination of clinical criteria [48].
text.formatted: In the categorical Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition, Text Revision (DSM-5-TR) classification, BPD is diagnosed through a specified combination of clinical criteria <ref type="bibr">[48]</ref>.

text.text: The Alternative Model for Personality Disorders (AMPD), presented in Section III of DSM-5-TR, incorporates dimensional assessments of self and interpersonal functioning and maladaptive personality traits, while retaining BPD as a diagnostic type.

Similarly, the International Classification of Diseases, 11th Revision (ICD-11) [4] emphasizes personality disorder severity and trait domains, while allowing an additional borderline pattern qualifier [49].
text.formatted: Similarly, the International Classification of Diseases, 11th Revision (ICD-11) <ref type="bibr">[4]</ref> emphasizes personality disorder severity and trait domains, while allowing an additional borderline pattern qualifier <ref type="bibr">[49]</ref>.

text.text: Kernberg's borderline personality organization and the borderline level of personality organization described in the Psychodynamic Diagnostic Manual, Second Edition (PDM-2) emphasize structural aspects of functioning, particularly identity integration, defensive functioning, and reality testing.
The PDM-2 additionally describes borderline personality as a style or type, distinct from the borderline level of organization [39, 50].
text.formatted: The PDM-2 additionally describes borderline personality as a style or type, distinct from the borderline level of organization <ref type="bibr">[39,</ref> <ref type="bibr">50]</ref>.

text.text: Within this psychoanalytic distinction, level of organization concerns the severity and structural integration of personality functioning, whereas style or type concerns its characteristic pattern.
Borderline organization may therefore underlie different personality styles and does not itself denote categorical BPD.
Although these frameworks describe overlapping clinical phenomena, they are not interchangeable.
Developmental explanations should therefore clearly specify whether they refer to a clinical pattern, dimensional impairment, or the underlying organization of personality.
Clarifying the outcomes to be explained also requires distinguishing the developmental roles assigned to different processes.

Within the theories reviewed above, antecedent vulnerabilities (characteristics that may increase subsequent risk without determining outcomes) may include emotional sensitivity and impulsivity; developmental conditions may include caregiving and other interpersonal experiences that may increase or reduce risk; and difficulties in emotion regulation, mentalization, or self-other representations may function as intervening processes, emerging manifestations, or factors contributing to the persistence of borderline pathology.
However, the same characteristic or process may be included in different categories across development.

In particular, moderators (factors that alter the relationship between developmental conditions and later outcomes) should be distinguished from mediators (hypothesized intervening processes that may explain such relationships).

Moreover, bidirectional causation requires specific testing, as observed associations may also reflect shared vulnerabilities, individual influences on the environment, or consequences of emerging psychopathology [19].
text.formatted: Moreover, bidirectional causation requires specific testing, as observed associations may also reflect shared vulnerabilities, individual influences on the environment, or consequences of emerging psychopathology <ref type="bibr">[19]</ref>.

text.text: Thus, the developmental accounts discussed here identify plausible relationships and competing interpretations, but their etiological significance depends on establishing temporal relationships and evaluating alternative explanations.

These theories and models provide a basis for examining how biology, epigenetics, environmental, social, and psychological factors may influence one another, while retaining distinctions among their proposed mechanisms and outcomes.
The following sections critically evaluate the corresponding evidence, distinguishing findings concerning BPD from broader developmental associations.
Section 7 then draws these findings together into possible developmental pathways and identifies testable propositions and directions for future research.
>Biological Foundations
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Biological Foundations</head>

text.text: Genetic contributions to BPD have been increasingly substantiated by both twin studies and largescale genomic research.

Heritability estimates suggest that approximately 0.35-0.65 of the variance in BPD traits can be attributed to genetic influences with a recent, large Swedish study estimating heritability of liability to diagnosed BPD at 0.46 (95% Confidence Interval [CI] = 0.39 -0.53) [51] and Amad et al. [52] reporting an estimated heritability of about 0.40.
text.formatted: Heritability estimates suggest that approximately 0.35-0.65 of the variance in BPD traits can be attributed to genetic influences with a recent, large Swedish study estimating heritability of liability to diagnosed BPD at 0.46 (95% Confidence Interval [CI] = 0.39 -0.53) <ref type="bibr">[51]</ref> and Amad et al. <ref type="bibr">[52]</ref> reporting an estimated heritability of about 0.40.

text.text: Skoglund et al. [51] found that full siblings of individuals diagnosed with BPD had a 4.7-fold higher hazard (95% CI = 3.9 -5.6) of receiving the same diagnosis compared to individuals without an affected sibling.
text.formatted: Skoglund et al. <ref type="bibr">[51]</ref> found that full siblings of individuals diagnosed with BPD had a 4.7-fold higher hazard (95% CI = 3.9 -5.6) of receiving the same diagnosis compared to individuals without an affected sibling.

text.text: For cousins whose parents were full siblings, the hazard was 1.7 fold higher (Hazard Ratio [HR] = 1.7; 95% CI = 1.4 -2.0).
Witt et al. [53] conducted the first case-control genome-wide association study (GWAS) of BPD.
text.formatted: Witt et al. <ref type="bibr">[53]</ref> conducted the first case-control genome-wide association study (GWAS) of BPD.

text.text: Gene-based analyses identified significant associations with DPYD, involved in uracil and thymidine metabolism and previously associated with schizophrenia (SCZ) and bipolar disorder (BP), and PKP4 (Plakophilin-4), involved in cell adhesion and cytoskeletal organization.
The previously reported association of serine incorporator 5 (SERINC5) with borderline personality features reached only nominal significance.
Streit et al. [54] published the largest GWAS meta-analysis to date of BPD.
text.formatted: Streit et al. <ref type="bibr">[54]</ref> published the largest GWAS meta-analysis to date of BPD.

text.text: They identified six genome-wide significant loci in the discovery analysis and five additional loci in the combined analysis, alongside nine genes in gene-based analyses; single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)-based heritability was estimated at 17.3% on the liability scale (in line with other psychiatric disorders where the SNP-based heritability is approximately one third of heritability estimates of twin studies).

Recent GWAS indicate that BPD shares significant genetic overlap with several major psychiatric disorders, including post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD; rg = 0.77), depression (rg = 0.74), attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD; rg = 0.67), SCZ (rg = 0.48), and BP (rg = 0.47).
Significant genetic correlations were also observed with loneliness, externalizing traits, neuroticism, chronic pain, antisocial behavior, and measures of suicide and self-harm.
Together, these findings support substantial transdiagnostic genetic liability and a polygenic, pleiotropic architecture, but do not establish mechanisms specific to BPD [54].
text.formatted: Together, these findings support substantial transdiagnostic genetic liability and a polygenic, pleiotropic architecture, but do not establish mechanisms specific to BPD <ref type="bibr">[54]</ref>.

text.text: Complementing molecular genetic findings, a large Swedish multigenerational study reported familial co-aggregation between BPD and multiple psychiatric conditions, including PTSD, depressive disorders, ADHD, other personality disorders, and drug use disorder, with contributions from both genetic and unique environmental factors [55].
text.formatted: Complementing molecular genetic findings, a large Swedish multigenerational study reported familial co-aggregation between BPD and multiple psychiatric conditions, including PTSD, depressive disorders, ADHD, other personality disorders, and drug use disorder, with contributions from both genetic and unique environmental factors <ref type="bibr">[55]</ref>.

text.text: Reflecting this complexity, research has advanced toward polygenic risk models and geneenvironment interaction frameworks, which may help clarify how biological predisposition interplays with developmental experiences [54, 56].
text.formatted: Reflecting this complexity, research has advanced toward polygenic risk models and geneenvironment interaction frameworks, which may help clarify how biological predisposition interplays with developmental experiences <ref type="bibr">[54,</ref> <ref type="bibr">56]</ref>.

text.text: Overall, genetic evidence supports substantial heritable liability to BPD, although the mechanisms linking genetic predisposition, developmental experiences, and divergent psychiatric outcomes remain insufficiently understood.

Neuroimaging studies of BPD report heterogeneous, task-dependent alterations in fronto-limbic activation, possible reductions in amygdala and hippocampal volumes, and reduced amygdala habituation associated with childhood adversity, without establishing a BPD-specific neural signature [57] [58] [59] [60] [61] [62] [63] [64] [65] [66].
text.formatted: Neuroimaging studies of BPD report heterogeneous, task-dependent alterations in fronto-limbic activation, possible reductions in amygdala and hippocampal volumes, and reduced amygdala habituation associated with childhood adversity, without establishing a BPD-specific neural signature <ref type="bibr">[57]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[58]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[59]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[60]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[61]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[62]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[63]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[64]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[65]</ref> <ref type="bibr">[66]</ref>.

text.text: In a longitudinal neuroimaging study, Constantino-Pettit et al. [67] found that lower estimated amygdala volume at age 13 was associated with greater borderline symptoms during adolescence, although whether this difference preceded symptom onset remains unclear.
text.formatted: In a longitudinal neuroimaging study, Constantino-Pettit et al. <ref type="bibr">[67]</ref> found that lower estimated amygdala volume at age 13 was associated with greater borderline symptoms during adolescence, although whether this difference preceded symptom onset remains unclear.

text.text: A detailed overview of these domains is provided in Supplementary Table 1.
text.formatted: A detailed overview of these domains is provided in Supplementary Table <ref type="table">1</ref>.

text.text: Future research should use larger, well-characterized, longitudinal samples integrating multimodal imaging with physiological and behavioral measures to determine whether neural alterations precede BPD onset, distinguish borderline trajectories from other psychiatric outcomes, and reflect enduring vulnerabilities rather than illness-related states.
Psychoneuroendocrine research shows that BPD is often accompanied by dysregulation of stressresponse systems.

Findings on hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis functioning are heterogeneous and depend partly on measurement methods, with meta-analytic evidence of increased continuous cortisol output but blunted responses to psychosocial stress.
Although early adversity may contribute to altered stress regulation, the underlying causal and epigenetic mechanisms remain uncertain [68] [69] [70] [71].
text.formatted: Although early adversity may contribute to altered stress regulation, the underlying causal and epigenetic mechanisms remain uncertain <ref type="bibr" target="#b67">[68]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">[69]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">[70]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">[71]</ref>.

text.text: A randomized placebo-controlled study found blunted cortisol responses to psychosocial stress despite greater subjective distress in women with BPD, while mineralocorticoid receptor stimulation reduced cortisol concentrations in both patients and healthy controls without supporting enhanced mineralocorticoid receptor-mediated feedback as the primary explanation for blunted stress responses in BPD [72].
text.formatted: A randomized placebo-controlled study found blunted cortisol responses to psychosocial stress despite greater subjective distress in women with BPD, while mineralocorticoid receptor stimulation reduced cortisol concentrations in both patients and healthy controls without supporting enhanced mineralocorticoid receptor-mediated feedback as the primary explanation for blunted stress responses in BPD <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">[72]</ref>.

text.text: Oxytocin-related findings in BPD suggest possible links with interpersonal functioning, but do not indicate a uniform biological alteration.

Lower plasma oxytocin concentrations and reduced oxytocin receptor expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells have been reported [73, 74], whereas a study of salivary oxytocin found no significant BPD-control difference [75].
text.formatted: Lower plasma oxytocin concentrations and reduced oxytocin receptor expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells have been reported <ref type="bibr" target="#b72">[73,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">74]</ref>, whereas a study of salivary oxytocin found no significant BPD-control difference <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">[75]</ref>.

text.text: Lower plasma oxytocin was associated with greater attachment-related preoccupation [74], while lower receptor expression, but not plasma oxytocin, was associated with overmentalization errors in a small BPD sample [76].
text.formatted: Lower plasma oxytocin was associated with greater attachment-related preoccupation <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">[74]</ref>, while lower receptor expression, but not plasma oxytocin, was associated with overmentalization errors in a small BPD sample <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">[76]</ref>.

text.text: Plasma oxytocin increased during psychotherapy in one study [74], but this observational change does not establish a treatment mechanism; intranasal oxytocin has also produced mixed interpersonal effects [17, 77].
text.formatted: Plasma oxytocin increased during psychotherapy in one study <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">[74]</ref>, but this observational change does not establish a treatment mechanism; intranasal oxytocin has also produced mixed interpersonal effects <ref type="bibr">[17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">77]</ref>.

text.text: Overall, differences in sampling, measurement, and interpersonal context limit mechanistic interpretation and BPD specificity; see Uzar et al. [77] for a recent review.
text.formatted: Overall, differences in sampling, measurement, and interpersonal context limit mechanistic interpretation and BPD specificity; see Uzar et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">[77]</ref> for a recent review.

text.text: Serotonergic candidate-gene studies have investigated associations between BPD and related clinical features, including impulsivity, suicidality, and affective instability, focusing on variants involving tryptophan hydroxylase 1 and 2 (TPH1/2), serotonin receptors 2A and 2C (HTR2A/C), and the serotonin-transporter-linked polymorphic region (5-HTTLPR) of SLC6A4, with some studies reporting positive findings [78] [79] [80] [81].
text.formatted: Serotonergic candidate-gene studies have investigated associations between BPD and related clinical features, including impulsivity, suicidality, and affective instability, focusing on variants involving tryptophan hydroxylase 1 and 2 (TPH1/2), serotonin receptors 2A and 2C (HTR2A/C), and the serotonin-transporter-linked polymorphic region (5-HTTLPR) of SLC6A4, with some studies reporting positive findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">[78]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">[79]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">[80]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">[81]</ref>.

text.text: However, findings are inconsistent, and meta-analytic evidence has not established significant associations for several commonly investigated serotonergic variants [52, 82].
text.formatted: However, findings are inconsistent, and meta-analytic evidence has not established significant associations for several commonly investigated serotonergic variants <ref type="bibr">[52,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">82]</ref>.

text.text: Exploratory genotype-stratified analyses suggested a possible gene-environment interaction involving 5-HTTLPR and serious life events in relation to impulsivity among patients with BPD [80].
text.formatted: Exploratory genotype-stratified analyses suggested a possible gene-environment interaction involving 5-HTTLPR and serious life events in relation to impulsivity among patients with BPD <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">[80]</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, evidence that this variant confers heightened sensitivity to both adverse and supportive environments, as predicted by differential susceptibility theory, remains insufficient [15, 56].
text.formatted: Nevertheless, evidence that this variant confers heightened sensitivity to both adverse and supportive environments, as predicted by differential susceptibility theory, remains insufficient <ref type="bibr">[15,</ref> <ref type="bibr">56]</ref>.

text.text: Preliminary findings suggest that oxytocin receptor gene variation may moderate the association between family environment and borderline symptoms, consistent with differential susceptibility (Figure 1) [17, 18].
text.formatted: Preliminary findings suggest that oxytocin receptor gene variation may moderate the association between family environment and borderline symptoms, consistent with differential susceptibility (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1</ref>) <ref type="bibr">[17,</ref> <ref type="bibr">18]</ref>.

text.text: Variants in catecholaminergic genes -including catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT), dopamine transporter (DAT1/SLC6A3), dopamine receptor D2 and D4 (DRD2/4), monoamine oxidase A (MAOA), dopamine-β-hydroxylase (DBH), and norepinephrine transporter (SLC6A2/NET) -have been studied in relation to BPD or related traits, with some studies reporting preliminary associations with emotional reactivity, impulsivity, and impulsive aggression [83] [84] [85] [86] [87] [88].
text.formatted: Variants in catecholaminergic genes -including catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT), dopamine transporter (DAT1/SLC6A3), dopamine receptor D2 and D4 (DRD2/4), monoamine oxidase A (MAOA), dopamine-β-hydroxylase (DBH), and norepinephrine transporter (SLC6A2/NET) -have been studied in relation to BPD or related traits, with some studies reporting preliminary associations with emotional reactivity, impulsivity, and impulsive aggression <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">[83]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">[84]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">[85]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">[86]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">[87]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">[88]</ref>.

text.text: Studies have also explored interactions between COMT, MAOA, and DBH variants and childhood adversity or other serious life events.
However, findings are inconsistent, and their implications for the etiological involvement of dopaminergic and noradrenergic systems remain uncertain [83, 84, 87, 88].
text.formatted: However, findings are inconsistent, and their implications for the etiological involvement of dopaminergic and noradrenergic systems remain uncertain <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">[83,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">84,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">87,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">88]</ref>.

text.text: Alterations in the endogenous opioid system, particularly involving μ-opioid receptors (MOR; OPRM1) and κ-opioid receptors (KOR; OPRK1), have been implicated in BPD.

A recent positron emission tomography (PET) study reported lower KOR tracer availability in several frontolimbic regions -including the amygdala, anterior cingulate, insula and hippocampus -in patients with BPD compared with healthy controls, alongside negative correlations between KOR availability and emotion dysregulation (awareness and clarity) within the BPD group, and impulsivity in the combined sample [89].
text.formatted: A recent positron emission tomography (PET) study reported lower KOR tracer availability in several frontolimbic regions -including the amygdala, anterior cingulate, insula and hippocampus -in patients with BPD compared with healthy controls, alongside negative correlations between KOR availability and emotion dysregulation (awareness and clarity) within the BPD group, and impulsivity in the combined sample <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">[89]</ref>.

text.text: Reduced MOR tone and KOR overactivity may contribute to dysphoria and stressrelated anhedonia, while OPRK1 hypomethylation associated with early neglect suggests a possible epigenetic mechanism [90, 91].
text.formatted: Reduced MOR tone and KOR overactivity may contribute to dysphoria and stressrelated anhedonia, while OPRK1 hypomethylation associated with early neglect suggests a possible epigenetic mechanism <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">[90,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">91]</ref>.

text.text: Some characteristic symptoms have been hypothesized to reflect unconscious attempts to stimulate the endogenous opioid system or consequences of its reduced activity [92], and opioid-receptor antagonists have shown possible benefits for dissociative and selfinjurious behaviors in uncontrolled reports, although two small placebo-controlled naltrexone trials (combined N = 29) found no statistically significant improvement over placebo in dissociative symptoms [93].
