text.text: A detailed overview of these neuroendocrine and neurochemical mechanisms is provided in Supplementary Table 1.
text.formatted: A detailed overview of these neuroendocrine and neurochemical mechanisms is provided in Supplementary Table <ref type="table">1</ref>.

text.text: Biological findings in BPD implicate stress-response, monoaminergic, and endogenous opioid systems, although their interactions and contributions to developmental vulnerability remain incompletely understood.

These findings are compatible with the clinical importance of trauma assessment and psychotherapeutic approaches addressing stress and emotion regulation, but do not establish specific causal mechanisms.

Findings on inflammation and oxidative stress in BPD are heterogeneous, with several studies reporting increased immune activation and oxidative imbalance, while one study identified a subgroup within a BPD sample with relatively elevated antioxidant and anti-inflammatory markers associated with longer illness duration and lower anxiety severity, potentially reflecting compensatory regulation.
Overall, these results suggest that immune and redox dysregulation may be associated with clinical features of BPD, but their causal contributions remain unestablished [94] [95] [96].
text.formatted: Overall, these results suggest that immune and redox dysregulation may be associated with clinical features of BPD, but their causal contributions remain unestablished <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">[94]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">[95]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">[96]</ref>.

text.text: A detailed overview of these domains is provided in Supplementary Table 1.
text.formatted: A detailed overview of these domains is provided in Supplementary Table <ref type="table">1</ref>.

text.text: These alterations, though heterogeneous, may converge with neuroendocrine and monoaminergic dysregulation to sustain chronic stress sensitivity and affective instability characteristic of BPD, potentially interacting with epigenetic processes through which environmental adversity may become biologically embedded [94, 95, 97, 98].
text.formatted: These alterations, though heterogeneous, may converge with neuroendocrine and monoaminergic dysregulation to sustain chronic stress sensitivity and affective instability characteristic of BPD, potentially interacting with epigenetic processes through which environmental adversity may become biologically embedded <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">[94,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">95,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">97,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">98]</ref>.

text.text: BPD is strongly associated with early-life adversity, making the study of epigenetic regulation relevant to understanding how environmental experiences may become biologically embedded.
Epigenetic processes can influence gene regulation without altering DNA sequence.

In BPD, differential methylation has been reported at selected loci involved in stress response, neurotransmission and neuroplasticity; however, these associations do not establish that adversityinduced epigenetic changes cause the disorder.
Epigenetic regulation includes DNA methylation, histone modifications that influence chromatin accessibility, and processes involving non-coding RNAs, such as microRNAs (miRNAs).
Direct research in BPD has focused predominantly on DNA methylation; evidence concerning histone modifications and non-coding RNAs is more limited.

Reported DNA methylation differences in BPD vary across loci, tissues, and studies, including findings involving genes implicated in stress response, neuroplasticity, and monoaminergic signaling, suggesting potential molecular pathways through which early stress exposure may shape emotional reactivity and behavioural regulation [97, [99] [100] [101] [102].
text.formatted: Reported DNA methylation differences in BPD vary across loci, tissues, and studies, including findings involving genes implicated in stress response, neuroplasticity, and monoaminergic signaling, suggesting potential molecular pathways through which early stress exposure may shape emotional reactivity and behavioural regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">[97,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">[99]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">[100]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">[101]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">[102]</ref>.

text.text: However, these pathways have not been causally established in BPD.

Treatment-associated changes involving brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and, in a small exploratory study, FK506-binding protein 5 (FKBP5) have been observed, but they do not demonstrate reversal of an etiological alteration [101] [102] [103].
text.formatted: Treatment-associated changes involving brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and, in a small exploratory study, FK506-binding protein 5 (FKBP5) have been observed, but they do not demonstrate reversal of an etiological alteration <ref type="bibr" target="#b100">[101]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">[102]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">[103]</ref>.

text.text: For example, BDNF methylation decreased among psychotherapy responders in one study although average methylation increased across the treated sample [102].
text.formatted: For example, BDNF methylation decreased among psychotherapy responders in one study although average methylation increased across the treated sample <ref type="bibr" target="#b101">[102]</ref>.

text.text: Another study observed decreased salivary but not blood BDNF methylation during treatment, without a correlation between methylation change and symptom improvement [103].
text.formatted: Another study observed decreased salivary but not blood BDNF methylation during treatment, without a correlation between methylation change and symptom improvement <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">[103]</ref>.

text.text: Supplementary Table 2 summarizes methylation findings observed in BPD samples, while Supplementary Table 3 summarizes the biological functions and hypothesized mechanistic or behavioral implications of genes investigated in DNA methylation studies involving BPD.
text.formatted: Supplementary Table <ref type="table">2</ref> summarizes methylation findings observed in BPD samples, while Supplementary Table <ref type="table">3</ref> summarizes the biological functions and hypothesized mechanistic or behavioral implications of genes investigated in DNA methylation studies involving BPD.

text.text: These findings are compatible with biological embedding but do not yet explain why similar adversity is followed by BPD in some individuals and by other disorders or no disorder in others.

Psychiatric-comparator studies improve assessment of specificity, but differences in adversity, comorbidity and other sample characteristics complicate interpretation; follow-up studies have also produced null findings and unsuccessful replications [98, [104] [105] [106].
text.formatted: Psychiatric-comparator studies improve assessment of specificity, but differences in adversity, comorbidity and other sample characteristics complicate interpretation; follow-up studies have also produced null findings and unsuccessful replications <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">[98,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b103">[104]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b104">[105]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b105">[106]</ref>.

text.text: Animal studies suggest that early-life stress can alter histone acetylation, with effects depending on genetic background and developmental context.
In mice, changes in histone H4 acetylation have been interpreted as potentially compensatory in relation to anxiety-and depressionlike behavior and antidepressant responsiveness [107].
text.formatted: In mice, changes in histone H4 acetylation have been interpreted as potentially compensatory in relation to anxiety-and depressionlike behavior and antidepressant responsiveness <ref type="bibr" target="#b106">[107]</ref>.

text.text: Research on depression and experimental models links histone-modifying enzymes, including histone deacetylases (HDACs) and histone acetyltransferases (HATs), to BDNF regulation and neuronal plasticity [108].
text.formatted: Research on depression and experimental models links histone-modifying enzymes, including histone deacetylases (HDACs) and histone acetyltransferases (HATs), to BDNF regulation and neuronal plasticity <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">[108]</ref>.

text.text: These findings provide general mechanistic context and suggest pathways that may also be relevant to BPD, although direct BPD-specific evidence remains limited.

Non-coding RNAs, particularly miRNAs, regulate post-transcriptional gene expression and have been implicated in stress-related processes in broader psychiatric and experimental research [109] [110] [111].
text.formatted: Non-coding RNAs, particularly miRNAs, regulate post-transcriptional gene expression and have been implicated in stress-related processes in broader psychiatric and experimental research <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">[109]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">[110]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">[111]</ref>.

text.text: In BPD, a genome-wide study reported methylation associations near MIR124-3 and MIR137 with diagnostic status and/or childhood maltreatment [98], while a separate exploratory study examined circulating miR-124-3p, globus pallidus (GP) volume, and spatial co-expression of target genes using reference brain-expression data [112].
text.formatted: In BPD, a genome-wide study reported methylation associations near MIR124-3 and MIR137 with diagnostic status and/or childhood maltreatment <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">[98]</ref>, while a separate exploratory study examined circulating miR-124-3p, globus pallidus (GP) volume, and spatial co-expression of target genes using reference brain-expression data <ref type="bibr" target="#b111">[112]</ref>.

text.text: Research outside BPD has implicated miRNAs in stress-related processes and psychiatric vulnerability [111, 113], while genetic findings have implicated the MIR137 locus and predicted miR-137 target genes in schizophrenia susceptibility [114].
text.formatted: Research outside BPD has implicated miRNAs in stress-related processes and psychiatric vulnerability <ref type="bibr" target="#b110">[111,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b112">113]</ref>, while genetic findings have implicated the MIR137 locus and predicted miR-137 target genes in schizophrenia susceptibility <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">[114]</ref>.

text.text: These findings provide a rationale for investigating the potential relevance of miR-137 to BPD, particularly its possible involvement in pathways linking environmental adversity, gene regulation, and psychiatric vulnerability.
Boström et al. [115] reported significant epigenetic age acceleration as measured by GrimAge in women with a history of suicide attempts and BPD compared with healthy controls.
text.formatted: Boström et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b114">[115]</ref> reported significant epigenetic age acceleration as measured by GrimAge in women with a history of suicide attempts and BPD compared with healthy controls.

text.text: Other epigenetic age measures did not show comparable group differences.

Notably, past alcohol or substance abuse, psychotropic medication use, self-reported exposure to violent behavior in youth or adulthood, later completed suicide, and age at first suicide attempt were not significantly associated with GrimAge acceleration within the BPD group in the reported analyses, whereas tobacco use showed a strong association.

These findings raise the possibility of altered biological aging in some individuals with BPD and motivate further research into how early adversity and other exposures relate to methylation-based aging measures.

Epigenetic research in BPD remains limited by small, often selected samples, reliance on peripheral tissues, variable adjustment for smoking, medication, comorbidity and cell composition, and inconsistent replication.
Predominantly cross-sectional designs leave uncertain whether observed methylation differences precede BPD or reflect environmental exposures, illness-related processes or treatment.

Although reported associations involve stress-response, neurotransmission and neuroplasticity pathways, candidate-gene selection partly shapes the evidence, and clinical validity and BPD specificity remain to be established.

Longitudinal studies beginning before symptom onset, with adversity-exposed and psychiatric comparison groups, independent replication and functional multi-omics analyses, could clarify the potential contribution of epigenetic processes to divergent developmental outcomes.

Environmental and social conditions are associated with BPD and borderline features across development, but the strength and interpretation of these associations depend on study design, clinical comparison groups, and whether the outcome is dimensional symptoms or diagnosed disorder.

This section evaluates childhood adversity, caregiving, peer environments, and broader social contexts as empirical antecedents or correlates rather than assuming that proposed developmental mechanisms have been causally established (Supplementary Table 4).
text.formatted: This section evaluates childhood adversity, caregiving, peer environments, and broader social contexts as empirical antecedents or correlates rather than assuming that proposed developmental mechanisms have been causally established (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">4</ref>).

text.text: Childhood adversity is frequently reported among individuals with BPD, although association magnitudes differ markedly across samples and designs.

In a meta-analysis of 97 studies, Porter et al. [116] estimated that 71.1% of participants with BPD in contributing samples reported at least one adverse childhood experience (ACE), based on prevalence data from 42 studies.
text.formatted: In a meta-analysis of 97 studies, Porter et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">[116]</ref> estimated that 71.1% of participants with BPD in contributing samples reported at least one adverse childhood experience (ACE), based on prevalence data from 42 studies.

text.text: Case-control comparisons found substantially higher odds of reported adversity among individuals with BPD than among nonclinical controls (odds ratio [OR] = 13.91, 95% CI = 11.11 -17.43) or other psychiatric groups (OR = 3.15, 95% CI = 2.62 -3.79).
These are exposure odds, not the risk of subsequently developing BPD [117].
text.formatted: These are exposure odds, not the risk of subsequently developing BPD <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">[117]</ref>.

text.text: Epidemiological analyses yielded a smaller estimate (OR = 2.56, 95% CI [1.24, 5.30]); the pooled cohort-study estimate was not statistically significant (OR = 2.59, 95% CI [0.93, 7.30]) [116].
text.formatted: Epidemiological analyses yielded a smaller estimate (OR = 2.56, 95% CI [1.24, 5.30]); the pooled cohort-study estimate was not statistically significant (OR = 2.59, 95% CI [0.93, 7.30]) <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">[116]</ref>.

text.text: Prospective etiological evidence remains considerably more limited than retrospective contrasts [116].
text.formatted: Prospective etiological evidence remains considerably more limited than retrospective contrasts <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">[116]</ref>.

text.text: Adversity type, co-occurrence, and measurement further complicate interpretation.

Emotional abuse and neglect produced large contrasts with nonclinical controls in Porter et al.'s [116] casecontrol analyses (OR = 38.11 and 17.73, respectively), but these estimates cannot be interpreted as independent causal contributions or as a stable ranking of risk factors.
text.formatted: Emotional abuse and neglect produced large contrasts with nonclinical controls in Porter et al.'s <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">[116]</ref> casecontrol analyses (OR = 38.11 and 17.73, respectively), but these estimates cannot be interpreted as independent causal contributions or as a stable ranking of risk factors.

text.text: In youth aged 19 years or younger, Winsper et al. [118] reported associations for sexual abuse (OR = 4.88), physical abuse (OR = 2.79), maternal hostility/verbal abuse (OR = 3.28), and neglect (OR = 3.40).
text.formatted: In youth aged 19 years or younger, Winsper et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b117">[118]</ref> reported associations for sexual abuse (OR = 4.88), physical abuse (OR = 2.79), maternal hostility/verbal abuse (OR = 3.28), and neglect (OR = 3.40).

text.text: Because adversity types are highly correlated and comparison groups and exposure instruments vary, meta-analytic subgroup differences should not be interpreted as causal rankings.

A multilevel meta-analysis found associations between childhood traumatic experiences and borderline features (pooled r=0.30) and between maladaptive parenting and such features (r=0.23), with generally smaller prospective than retrospective estimates [119].
text.formatted: A multilevel meta-analysis found associations between childhood traumatic experiences and borderline features (pooled r=0.30) and between maladaptive parenting and such features (r=0.23), with generally smaller prospective than retrospective estimates <ref type="bibr" target="#b118">[119]</ref>.

text.text: Associations involving emotional abuse and neglect, together with the findings of Schulze et al. [120], highlight chronic relational adversity as a relevant area of investigation in borderline pathology.
text.formatted: Associations involving emotional abuse and neglect, together with the findings of Schulze et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">[120]</ref>, highlight chronic relational adversity as a relevant area of investigation in borderline pathology.

text.text: Emerging evidence points to potential psychological pathways linking ACEs to BPD features.

Emotion dysregulation has been identified as a statistical mediator of associations between childhood abuse and BPD features, as well as broader personality disorder traits [121], although the corresponding indirect associations were not found for a broader ACE composite in the study's transdiagnostic analysis.
text.formatted: Emotion dysregulation has been identified as a statistical mediator of associations between childhood abuse and BPD features, as well as broader personality disorder traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b120">[121]</ref>, although the corresponding indirect associations were not found for a broader ACE composite in the study's transdiagnostic analysis.

text.text: Schulze et al. [120] further reported that emotional abuse may serve as a key link between ACEs and BPD features, while identity disturbance was associated with attachment anxiety; attachment and perceived social support partly accounted for the adversity-BPD association.
text.formatted: Schulze et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b119">[120]</ref> further reported that emotional abuse may serve as a key link between ACEs and BPD features, while identity disturbance was associated with attachment anxiety; attachment and perceived social support partly accounted for the adversity-BPD association.

text.text: Yuan et al. [122] also support the importance of emotional abuse as an independently associated maltreatment subtype, with emotion dysregulation statistically mediating part of the maltreatment-BPD feature association.
text.formatted: Yuan et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b121">[122]</ref> also support the importance of emotional abuse as an independently associated maltreatment subtype, with emotion dysregulation statistically mediating part of the maltreatment-BPD feature association.

text.text: Schmitz et al. [123] suggest that body dissociation might be a potential link between ACEs and emotion regulation.
text.formatted: Schmitz et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b122">[123]</ref> suggest that body dissociation might be a potential link between ACEs and emotion regulation.

text.text: They found lower levels of body awareness and higher levels of body dissociation in BPD patients in comparison to healthy controls.
Body dissociation was positively associated with childhood trauma and emotion dysregulation and statistically mediated their association within the BPD group.

Taken together, these findings highlight emotional abuse and neglect potentially as important forms of relational adversity associated with borderline pathology, with emotion dysregulation emerging as a candidate intervening process.
Additional associated processes, such as attachment anxiety and body dissociation, further suggest possible pathways through which early adversity may relate to later psychological functioning.
However, these predominantly cross-sectional findings do not establish causal developmental mediation or BPDspecific protective effects of social support.
More recently, Vonderlin et al. [124] assessed co-occurring adverse experiences in BPD, psychiatric-control, and nonclinical groups.
text.formatted: More recently, Vonderlin et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">[124]</ref> assessed co-occurring adverse experiences in BPD, psychiatric-control, and nonclinical groups.

text.text: Emotional abuse, bullying, parental unpredictability, and lack of safety showed conditional associations with current BPD symptom severity, but the crosssectional network cannot establish temporal order or BPD-specific causes.
These environmental influences intersect with genetic, neurobiological, and epigenetic pathways relevant to personality development and vulnerability to BPD [125].
text.formatted: These environmental influences intersect with genetic, neurobiological, and epigenetic pathways relevant to personality development and vulnerability to BPD <ref type="bibr" target="#b124">[125]</ref>.

text.text: Clinically, BPD and cPTSD show partial symptom overlap but distinct underlying configurations [5].
text.formatted: Clinically, BPD and cPTSD show partial symptom overlap but distinct underlying configurations <ref type="bibr">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Nevertheless, it is possible that cPTSD overlaps with some presentations characterized by persistent subsyndromal BPD features [126], particularly when interpersonal avoidance rather than pronounced interpersonal instability predominates.
text.formatted: Nevertheless, it is possible that cPTSD overlaps with some presentations characterized by persistent subsyndromal BPD features <ref type="bibr" target="#b125">[126]</ref>, particularly when interpersonal avoidance rather than pronounced interpersonal instability predominates.

text.text: However, this possibility remains a diagnostic hypothesis rather than an established equivalence between the two conditions [127].
text.formatted: However, this possibility remains a diagnostic hypothesis rather than an established equivalence between the two conditions <ref type="bibr" target="#b126">[127]</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, trauma is neither necessary nor sufficient for the development of BPD.

In a qualitative study of 12 pairs of sisters reporting comparable childhood maltreatment, sisters without current psychopathology described greater emotion-regulation capacities, future orientation, and access to supportive relationships than their sisters with BPD.
These retrospective accounts identify possible protective processes but do not establish their temporal or causal roles [128].
text.formatted: These retrospective accounts identify possible protective processes but do not establish their temporal or causal roles <ref type="bibr" target="#b127">[128]</ref>.

text.text: A scoping review likewise identified associations between lower resilience scores and borderline pathology, but heterogeneous measures and limited longitudinal evidence leave unresolved whether reduced resilience precedes or follows BPD [129].
text.formatted: A scoping review likewise identified associations between lower resilience scores and borderline pathology, but heterogeneous measures and limited longitudinal evidence leave unresolved whether reduced resilience precedes or follows BPD <ref type="bibr" target="#b128">[129]</ref>.

text.text: Genetic, temperamental, and environmental factors may interact to shape development, although the specific developmental processes linking adversity to borderline pathology remain incompletely understood.
Prospective multi-informant research is needed to distinguish antecedent vulnerabilities, environmental exposures, intervening processes, and alternative psychiatric or adaptive outcomes [2, 130].
text.formatted: Prospective multi-informant research is needed to distinguish antecedent vulnerabilities, environmental exposures, intervening processes, and alternative psychiatric or adaptive outcomes <ref type="bibr">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b129">130]</ref>.

text.text: The early caregiver-child relationship is central to personality development, and attachment difficulties are frequently associated with BPD.

Individuals with BPD commonly exhibit insecure or disorganized attachment patterns, which may be associated with histories of inconsistent, frightening, or emotionally unsupportive caregiving, although these associations do not establish developmental causation [35, 131, 132].
text.formatted: Individuals with BPD commonly exhibit insecure or disorganized attachment patterns, which may be associated with histories of inconsistent, frightening, or emotionally unsupportive caregiving, although these associations do not establish developmental causation <ref type="bibr">[35,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b130">131,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b131">132]</ref>.

text.text: A meta-analysis of adult romantic attachment found that attachment anxiety is strongly correlated with BPD traits (r = 0.48), while attachment avoidance also shows a significant, albeit smaller, association (r = 0.30), without establishing whether these patterns originated in early caregiving experiences [133].
text.formatted: A meta-analysis of adult romantic attachment found that attachment anxiety is strongly correlated with BPD traits (r = 0.48), while attachment avoidance also shows a significant, albeit smaller, association (r = 0.30), without establishing whether these patterns originated in early caregiving experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b132">[133]</ref>.

text.text: Prospective community-based evidence suggests that prenatal family adversity, maladaptive parenting practices, and high parental conflict in childhood are associated with a greater likelihood of borderline symptoms by early adolescence, supporting the potential developmental relevance of family environments without establishing a causal pathway [134].
text.formatted: Prospective community-based evidence suggests that prenatal family adversity, maladaptive parenting practices, and high parental conflict in childhood are associated with a greater likelihood of borderline symptoms by early adolescence, supporting the potential developmental relevance of family environments without establishing a causal pathway <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">[134]</ref>.

text.text: Parental psychopathology is also associated with offspring borderline features, including findings involving parental substance dependence, maternal depression, antisocial pathology, and borderline traits [135, 136], although parental depression and antisocial behavior did not predict adolescent borderline symptom trajectories in another longitudinal study [137].
text.formatted: Parental psychopathology is also associated with offspring borderline features, including findings involving parental substance dependence, maternal depression, antisocial pathology, and borderline traits <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">[135,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b135">136]</ref>, although parental depression and antisocial behavior did not predict adolescent borderline symptom trajectories in another longitudinal study <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">[137]</ref>.

text.text: Familial transmission may involve both genetic and environmental contributions, including adverse caregiving, with their relative importance varying across parental characteristics and family contexts [136].
text.formatted: Familial transmission may involve both genetic and environmental contributions, including adverse caregiving, with their relative importance varying across parental characteristics and family contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b135">[136]</ref>.

text.text: Parental emotional unavailability and neglect, maternal and paternal invalidation, maternal inconsistency, hostility and emotional overinvolvement, low warmth, boundary dissolution, family life stress, maternal and paternal conflict, and harsh punishment have been investigated as potential antecedents or correlates of borderline features, although prospective evidence varies across these factors [134, [137] [138] [139].
text.formatted: Parental emotional unavailability and neglect, maternal and paternal invalidation, maternal inconsistency, hostility and emotional overinvolvement, low warmth, boundary dissolution, family life stress, maternal and paternal conflict, and harsh punishment have been investigated as potential antecedents or correlates of borderline features, although prospective evidence varies across these factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b133">[134,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">[137]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b137">[138]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">[139]</ref>.

text.text: Patients frequently retrospectively describe their parents as overinvolved, indifferent, neglectful, or invalidating, and often recall a home atmosphere experienced as conflictual or inconsistent [137] [138] [139].
text.formatted: Patients frequently retrospectively describe their parents as overinvolved, indifferent, neglectful, or invalidating, and often recall a home atmosphere experienced as conflictual or inconsistent <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">[137]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b137">[138]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">[139]</ref>.

text.text: However, retrospective reports cannot independently establish the temporal or causal role of these experiences.

Adoption and twin-family comparisons found associations between maternal BPD traits, adverse caregiving, and offspring borderline features in both biological and adoptive families, consistent with environmental contributions.
In contrast, associations involving paternal BPD traits and parental externalizing psychopathology were more consistent with genetic transmission [136].
text.formatted: In contrast, associations involving paternal BPD traits and parental externalizing psychopathology were more consistent with genetic transmission <ref type="bibr" target="#b135">[136]</ref>.

text.text: However, in a complementary observational study, Bunz et al. [140] found no significant differences in observed adaptive emotion-regulation strategies among 318 young children of mothers with BPD, mothers with anxiety or depressive disorders, and healthy controls, while maladaptive strategies were too infrequent for meaningful group comparisons; later developmental differences remain possible.
text.formatted: However, in a complementary observational study, Bunz et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b139">[140]</ref> found no significant differences in observed adaptive emotion-regulation strategies among 318 young children of mothers with BPD, mothers with anxiety or depressive disorders, and healthy controls, while maladaptive strategies were too infrequent for meaningful group comparisons; later developmental differences remain possible.

text.text: Maternal interpersonal emotion regulation strategies were associated with adolescent BPD symptom severity: the association between adolescent negative affect and BPD severity was stronger when maternal problem-solving was high but support/validation was low, and attenuated when support/validation was higher.
However, these measures did not predict subsequent changes in BPD symptoms [141].
text.formatted: However, these measures did not predict subsequent changes in BPD symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b140">[141]</ref>.

text.text: Parent-child interactions are bidirectional, as adolescent behavior can also predict subsequent changes in parental responses [142], with reciprocal associations also reported between parenting and adolescent borderline features [137].
text.formatted: Parent-child interactions are bidirectional, as adolescent behavior can also predict subsequent changes in parental responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b141">[142]</ref>, with reciprocal associations also reported between parenting and adolescent borderline features <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">[137]</ref>.

text.text: Exposure to interparental intimate partner violence has been prospectively associated with elevated adolescent borderline features and slower subsequent declines [143], while adult studies link borderline traits with both intimate partner violence perpetration and victimization [144], suggesting that interpersonal violence may represent both a developmental antecedent and a perpetuating interpersonal context.
text.formatted: Exposure to interparental intimate partner violence has been prospectively associated with elevated adolescent borderline features and slower subsequent declines <ref type="bibr" target="#b142">[143]</ref>, while adult studies link borderline traits with both intimate partner violence perpetration and victimization <ref type="bibr" target="#b143">[144]</ref>, suggesting that interpersonal violence may represent both a developmental antecedent and a perpetuating interpersonal context.

text.text: Relationship discord and lack of closeness with parents are also associated with impaired adolescent personality functioning [145].
text.formatted: Relationship discord and lack of closeness with parents are also associated with impaired adolescent personality functioning <ref type="bibr" target="#b144">[145]</ref>.

text.text: Conversely, perceived parental closeness is associated with lower BPD severity, with lower identity diffusion potentially accounting for part of this association [146].
text.formatted: Conversely, perceived parental closeness is associated with lower BPD severity, with lower identity diffusion potentially accounting for part of this association <ref type="bibr" target="#b145">[146]</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, genetic or temperamental vulnerabilities may interact with caregiving environments marked by psychopathology, invalidation, or violence in the development of borderline features.

A large meta-analysis reported findings broadly consistent with transactional accounts, including associations involving early psychopathology, invalidating experiences, and emotionregulation difficulties [119].
text.formatted: A large meta-analysis reported findings broadly consistent with transactional accounts, including associations involving early psychopathology, invalidating experiences, and emotionregulation difficulties <ref type="bibr" target="#b118">[119]</ref>.

text.text: Longitudinal evidence associates specific family experiences, including exposure to interparental violence and poorer father-adolescent relationship quality, with less favorable trajectories of adolescent borderline features; evidence that other assessed parenting practices predict symptom persistence or that maternal support/validation mitigates progression remains limited [147].
text.formatted: Longitudinal evidence associates specific family experiences, including exposure to interparental violence and poorer father-adolescent relationship quality, with less favorable trajectories of adolescent borderline features; evidence that other assessed parenting practices predict symptom persistence or that maternal support/validation mitigates progression remains limited <ref type="bibr" target="#b146">[147]</ref>.

text.text: Broader social contexts -peer, school, and community environments -further shape whether these vulnerabilities are reinforced or attenuated.

Peer experiences may contribute to the developmental context of borderline pathology, but findings concerning environmental antecedents must be distinguished from interpersonal difficulties accompanying existing borderline features.

A scoping review of 39 studies identified associations between borderline features and difficulties involving friendships, peer victimization, and aggression; only eight studies examined more than one peer domain, limiting conclusions about their interrelationships and developmental direction [148].
text.formatted: A scoping review of 39 studies identified associations between borderline features and difficulties involving friendships, peer victimization, and aggression; only eight studies examined more than one peer domain, limiting conclusions about their interrelationships and developmental direction <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">[148]</ref>.

text.text: Prospective research suggests that individual characteristics may precede both later peer difficulties and borderline features.

In a longitudinal cohort of 153 children, lower preschool conscientiousness showed nominal associations with poorer school-age peer relationships and higher adolescent borderline features, but these associations did not survive correction for multiple testing, and mediation through peer relationships was not supported [149].
text.formatted: In a longitudinal cohort of 153 children, lower preschool conscientiousness showed nominal associations with poorer school-age peer relationships and higher adolescent borderline features, but these associations did not survive correction for multiple testing, and mediation through peer relationships was not supported <ref type="bibr" target="#b148">[149]</ref>.

text.text: Chronic school-behavior stress in adolescence has been prospectively associated with BPD symptoms in young adulthood, whereas peer-relationship stress did not remain independently associated after adjustment for other risk factors [150].
text.formatted: Chronic school-behavior stress in adolescence has been prospectively associated with BPD symptoms in young adulthood, whereas peer-relationship stress did not remain independently associated after adjustment for other risk factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b149">[150]</ref>.

text.text: Individuals with BPD features often struggle to form and maintain friendships, reporting lower perceived support and greater conflict [148].
text.formatted: Individuals with BPD features often struggle to form and maintain friendships, reporting lower perceived support and greater conflict <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">[148]</ref>.

text.text: In one adolescent study, borderline characteristics were associated with less friendship support among boys and greater friendship conflict among both boys and girls [148].
text.formatted: In one adolescent study, borderline characteristics were associated with less friendship support among boys and greater friendship conflict among both boys and girls <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">[148]</ref>.

text.text: Peer functioning may improve following treatment; a small uncontrolled study reported improved peer attachment after a one-year program of group-based mentalization-based treatment (MBT) [148, 151].
text.formatted: Peer functioning may improve following treatment; a small uncontrolled study reported improved peer attachment after a one-year program of group-based mentalization-based treatment (MBT) <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">[148,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b150">151]</ref>.

text.text: Bullying victimization is associated with borderline features [148].
text.formatted: Bullying victimization is associated with borderline features <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">[148]</ref>.

text.text: Longitudinal data indicate that victimization -but not perpetration -statistically mediates part of the continuity of borderline traits from childhood to adolescence [152].
text.formatted: Longitudinal data indicate that victimization -but not perpetration -statistically mediates part of the continuity of borderline traits from childhood to adolescence <ref type="bibr" target="#b151">[152]</ref>.

text.text: Findings from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC) cohort (n = 6050; 51.4% female) show that chronic self-reported bullying victimization was associated with more than fivefold higher odds of exhibiting five or more BPD symptoms at approximately age 12 (OR = 5.44; 95% CI, 3.86-7.66), after adjustment for measured confounders [153].
text.formatted: Findings from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC) cohort (n = 6050; 51.4% female) show that chronic self-reported bullying victimization was associated with more than fivefold higher odds of exhibiting five or more BPD symptoms at approximately age 12 (OR = 5.44; 95% CI, 3.86-7.66), after adjustment for measured confounders <ref type="bibr" target="#b152">[153]</ref>.

text.text: In another analysis of overlapping ALSPAC participants, children with greater behavioral dysregulation were more likely to experience bullying, which was subsequently associated with borderline symptoms.
This indirect statistical association was significantly stronger for borderline symptoms than for depressive or psychotic symptoms, but was not unique to BPD [154].
text.formatted: This indirect statistical association was significantly stronger for borderline symptoms than for depressive or psychotic symptoms, but was not unique to BPD <ref type="bibr" target="#b153">[154]</ref>.

text.text: Interpersonal violence and relational adversity may also be relevant to BPD development.

Adolescent dating violence victimization has been prospectively associated with later internalizing and externalizing symptoms, substance use, and revictimization in general adolescent samples, although findings vary across studies [155].
text.formatted: Adolescent dating violence victimization has been prospectively associated with later internalizing and externalizing symptoms, substance use, and revictimization in general adolescent samples, although findings vary across studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b154">[155]</ref>.

text.text: In a five-year longitudinal study of 818 adolescent daters, borderline features prospectively predicted relational, psychological, and physical dating-violence victimization, primarily among girls, whereas psychological victimization predicted later borderline features more consistently among boys, and sexual victimization predicted later borderline features among girls [156].

text.text: Prospective studies suggest associations in both temporal directions between borderline features and peer victimization.

Children with borderline features at age 12 were more likely to experience peer and cyber-victimization by age 18, even after controlling for emotional and behavioral problems [158], although genetically informative analyses implicated shared genetic liability in many associations with adverse outcomes.

text.text: Beyond interpersonal dynamics, socioeconomic disadvantage adds another layer of vulnerability.
Low socioeconomic status (SES), including receipt of social assistance, predicts later borderline features across multiple studies [2].

text.formatted: Low childhood executive functioning also predicts later BPD diagnosis, while an exploratory interaction with low SES was associated with higher dimensional borderline features <ref type="bibr" target="#b162">[163]</ref>.

text.formatted: In one longitudinal cohort, African American girls and those living in poverty had higher average BPD symptom levels during adolescence <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">[137]</ref>.

text.text: Communitylevel data reveal that the treated incidence of borderline personality pathology was higher in more socially fragmented neighborhoods and certain categories of socioeconomic deprivation, although these findings do not establish effects on disorder onset [164].
text.formatted: Communitylevel data reveal that the treated incidence of borderline personality pathology was higher in more socially fragmented neighborhoods and certain categories of socioeconomic deprivation, although these findings do not establish effects on disorder onset <ref type="bibr" target="#b163">[164]</ref>.

text.text: In adult women with BPD, greater shame and a relatively more shame-prone implicit self-concept have been reported, alongside associations between shame-proneness and lower self-esteem [167].

text.text: Conceptually, the relational findings reviewed above are compatible with transactional developmental models, in which individual vulnerabilities and environmental experiences may influence one another over time [13, 137].
text.formatted: Conceptually, the relational findings reviewed above are compatible with transactional developmental models, in which individual vulnerabilities and environmental experiences may influence one another over time <ref type="bibr">[13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">137]</ref>.

text.text: Over time, these reciprocal interactions may compound psychological burden and contribute to a more persistent course of borderline pathology in some individuals.
In sum, environmental and social contexts may contribute to developmental vulnerability to BPD.

Evidence from peer victimization and socioeconomic adversity, alongside findings concerning cultural influences on symptom expression and recognition, highlights the relevance of broader social environments, although their cumulative interactions and causal contributions remain uncertain [2, 148].
text.formatted: Evidence from peer victimization and socioeconomic adversity, alongside findings concerning cultural influences on symptom expression and recognition, highlights the relevance of broader social environments, although their cumulative interactions and causal contributions remain uncertain <ref type="bibr">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">148]</ref>.

text.text: Etiological models should consider social contexts alongside familial and individual factors, including potential protective influences that require further investigation.
Such environments may inform prevention research and psychotherapeutic approaches, although whether modifying them reduces BPD incidence remains to be established.
Although biological, epigenetic, and environmental factors have been implicated in BPD, their potential influences may converge within psychological functioning.
This dimension reflects how temperament, early relationships, and defensive adaptations shape enduring patterns of thought, emotion, and behavior.
Together, these perspectives suggest how psychological mechanisms may mediate biological and social influences, contributing to the chronic instability characteristic of BPD.

As discussed in Section 2, attachment and schema theories propose that insecure and disorganized attachment associated with inconsistent or frightening caregiving may contribute to lasting psychological vulnerability.
Children may develop internal working models of self as unworthy of care and of others as unreliable or rejecting [132].
text.formatted: Children may develop internal working models of self as unworthy of care and of others as unreliable or rejecting <ref type="bibr" target="#b131">[132]</ref>.

text.text: Over time, these models may contribute to maladaptive cognitive schemas -abandonment, mistrust, or defectiveness -that shape perception and emotion in later relationships [41].
text.formatted: Over time, these models may contribute to maladaptive cognitive schemas -abandonment, mistrust, or defectiveness -that shape perception and emotion in later relationships <ref type="bibr">[41]</ref>.

text.text: Attachment ruptures may therefore form part of the developmental ground for enduring schema-level vulnerabilities linking early adversity to BPD vulnerability.
However, the cited evidence does not establish this complete developmental sequence.
Temperament adds another layer of vulnerability.
It reflects biologically based tendencies in emotional and behavioral response.
Longitudinal studies link impulsivity, aggression, and dysregulation -as well as ADHD and oppositional symptoms -to later BPD features [2, 172, 173].
text.formatted: Longitudinal studies link impulsivity, aggression, and dysregulation -as well as ADHD and oppositional symptoms -to later BPD features <ref type="bibr">[2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b171">172,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b172">173]</ref>.

text.text: These findings suggest an early diathesis paralleling the biological risks discussed earlier.
In adolescence, emerging borderline features often co-occur with substance use, eating disorders, and self-injury [13, 174].
text.formatted: In adolescence, emerging borderline features often co-occur with substance use, eating disorders, and self-injury <ref type="bibr">[13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b173">174]</ref>.

text.text: Prospective associations with internalizing and externalizing psychopathology vary across studies [2].
text.formatted: Prospective associations with internalizing and externalizing psychopathology vary across studies <ref type="bibr">[2]</ref>.

text.text: In a prospective study of girls, poor behavioral control and interpersonal difficulties helped distinguish predictor profiles for later borderline versus depressive symptoms, while mood/anxiety difficulties and parenting patterns differentiated borderline from conduct-symptom profiles [175].
text.formatted: In a prospective study of girls, poor behavioral control and interpersonal difficulties helped distinguish predictor profiles for later borderline versus depressive symptoms, while mood/anxiety difficulties and parenting patterns differentiated borderline from conduct-symptom profiles <ref type="bibr" target="#b174">[175]</ref>.

text.text: These findings concern prediction of later symptom levels, rather than new onset or established causal pathways.

A large longitudinal twin study found that common genetic influences substantially accounted for associations between retrospectively reported childhood abuse and adult borderline traits, although small nonshared environmental associations remained [172].
text.formatted: A large longitudinal twin study found that common genetic influences substantially accounted for associations between retrospectively reported childhood abuse and adult borderline traits, although small nonshared environmental associations remained <ref type="bibr" target="#b171">[172]</ref>.

text.text: These findings provided little support for a causal effect in this sample, but retrospective abuse reporting and assessment of borderline traits rather than diagnosed BPD limit broader conclusions about maltreatment's etiological role.

Other genetically informed studies have yielded mixed findings: Skaug et al. [176] similarly found little support for a causal effect of childhood trauma on borderline traits, whereas Belsky et al. [177] and Arneberg et al. [178] found associations that persisted after accounting for genetic and environmental factors shared by twins, although they examined childhood borderline-related characteristics and broader stressful life events, respectively.
text.formatted: Other genetically informed studies have yielded mixed findings: Skaug et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b175">[176]</ref> similarly found little support for a causal effect of childhood trauma on borderline traits, whereas Belsky et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b176">[177]</ref> and Arneberg et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b177">[178]</ref> found associations that persisted after accounting for genetic and environmental factors shared by twins, although they examined childhood borderline-related characteristics and broader stressful life events, respectively.

text.text: Taken together, these studies suggest that shared genetic and environmental influences explain part -and, in some studies, much -of the association between adversity and borderline features, while findings concerning an additional causal contribution of adversity remain mixed.
Adversity therefore remains a plausible developmental contributor, but its causal role cannot be inferred from the strength of its association with BPD alone.
These developmental observations are complemented by trait-based personality research.
BPD is associated with a Big Five personality profile of high Neuroticism and low Agreeableness and Conscientiousness.
Extraversion also tends to be lower, while Openness shows mixed results [179] [180] [181] [182].

text.text: GWAS data show a significant genetic correlation between BPD and Neuroticism (rg = 0.34) and a nominally significant correlation with Openness (rg = 0.24), but no statistically significant correlations were detected with the other traits [183].

text.text: Twin-family data similarly report strong positive associations of borderline personality features with Neuroticism (r = 0.68) and moderate negative ones with Agreeableness and Conscientiousness.
Much of this overlap reflects shared genetic influences, especially Neuroticism [184].
text.formatted: Much of this overlap reflects shared genetic influences, especially Neuroticism <ref type="bibr" target="#b183">[184]</ref>.

text.text: Personality traits show lower rank-order stability in BPD than in other personality disorders, particularly Neuroticism and Conscientiousness [185].
text.formatted: Personality traits show lower rank-order stability in BPD than in other personality disorders, particularly Neuroticism and Conscientiousness <ref type="bibr" target="#b184">[185]</ref>.

text.text: Alternative models offer complementary descriptions.
Research using Cloninger's Temperament and Character Inventory (TCI) associates borderline pathology with higher Novelty Seeking [187].
text.formatted: Research using Cloninger's Temperament and Character Inventory (TCI) associates borderline pathology with higher Novelty Seeking <ref type="bibr" target="#b186">[187]</ref>.

text.text: Temperament operates within reciprocal dynamics.

As discussed in Section 2, children's emotional responses and caregiving may influence one another, although evidence for greater responsiveness to both adverse and supportive environments specifically in BPD development remains limited.
Cognitive models propose that early vulnerabilities may contribute to maladaptive cognitive schemas -enduring beliefs about self, others, and the world [41].
text.formatted: Cognitive models propose that early vulnerabilities may contribute to maladaptive cognitive schemas -enduring beliefs about self, others, and the world <ref type="bibr">[41]</ref>.

text.text: Individuals with BPD often hold schemas of unlovability, abandonment, or defectiveness that shape perception and emotion.
Maladaptive schemas are elevated relative to healthy controls but also occur across other disorders [189].
text.formatted: Maladaptive schemas are elevated relative to healthy controls but also occur across other disorders <ref type="bibr" target="#b188">[189]</ref>.

text.text: An experimental study found negative interpersonal evaluations without consistent evidence of dichotomous thinking in the task used [190].
text.formatted: An experimental study found negative interpersonal evaluations without consistent evidence of dichotomous thinking in the task used <ref type="bibr" target="#b189">[190]</ref>.

text.text: An e-diary study found greater self-esteem instability in BPD than in anxiety disorders and healthy controls, whereas affective instability did not distinguish the two clinical groups [191].
text.formatted: An e-diary study found greater self-esteem instability in BPD than in anxiety disorders and healthy controls, whereas affective instability did not distinguish the two clinical groups <ref type="bibr" target="#b190">[191]</ref>.

text.text: This finding does not establish a developmental pathway or equate selfesteem instability with identity disturbance.
In sum, temperament, trait dispositions, and maladaptive schemas may contribute to BPD vulnerability and persistence.
Whether their combinations or developmental sequences distinguish BPD from other outcomes remains unresolved.
Psychodynamic theories have long linked borderline pathology to early relational development.
Kernberg [39] emphasized splitting, identity diffusion, and difficulties integrating self-other representations, as discussed in Section 2.

text.formatted: However, a meta-analysis found no significantly stronger association between hypermentalizing and BPD than between hypermentalizing and other psychopathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b198">[199]</ref>.

text.text: This pattern is consistent with aspects of mentalization-based formulations but does not establish the proposed developmental pathway from early attachment disturbances to impaired reflective functioning and BPD.
In sum, psychodynamic theories emphasize disturbances in self-experience and relationships alongside emotional dysregulation, while differing in their proposed mechanisms.
These perspectives complement the examination of emotional and behavioral regulation that follows.
Central to BPD's psychology is difficulty regulating intense emotions.
Individuals with BPD experience rapid and extreme mood shifts -e.g. plunging from calm to despair or rage within minutes in response to a perceived slight [13].
text.formatted: Individuals with BPD experience rapid and extreme mood shifts -e.g. plunging from calm to despair or rage within minutes in response to a perceived slight <ref type="bibr">[13]</ref>.

text.text: An experience-sampling study also found that arousal predicted subsequent perceived rejection, without significant differences in this temporal association between BPD, depressive disorders, and healthy controls [200].
text.formatted: An experience-sampling study also found that arousal predicted subsequent perceived rejection, without significant differences in this temporal association between BPD, depressive disorders, and healthy controls <ref type="bibr" target="#b199">[200]</ref>.

text.text: Compared with healthy controls, individuals with BPD report relying less on adaptive emotion regulation strategies (reappraisal, problem solving, acceptance) and more on maladaptive ones (suppression, rumination, avoidance); compared with other psychiatric groups, they report greater rumination and avoidance and lower problem solving and acceptance [201].

Findings on facial emotion recognition in BPD are mixed [204].

Impulsive behavior may occur in response to strong affect [209].

text.text: In summary, BPD is associated with difficulties in emotional regulation, impulse control, and interpersonal functioning.
Their possible developmental interactions are considered in Section 7.
These accounts suggest one or more possible developmental courses toward BPD.
Early in development, genetic, epigenetic, and prenatal influences may contribute to differences in emotional reactivity, recovery from arousal, activity, and emerging behavioral regulation.
However, these characteristics do not necessarily lead to later BPD.
Environmental factors may also influence biological development.

The relevance of these early differences to borderline development may depend on reciprocal exchanges with caregivers and broader social environments, alongside the development of psychological capacities and ways of experiencing oneself.

Within this framework, adversity-related pathways are proposed rather than established: genetically informed findings are mixed, and shared liabilities may account for part of the associations attributed to environmental experience (see Section 6.1).
Infants' characteristics and caregivers' capacities and circumstances jointly shape recurring exchanges.
Greater emotional sensitivity or difficulty being soothed may increase demands for external regulation, while caregiver responses may ease distress, increase it, or inhibit its expression.
When the child is consistently invalidated or cannot rely on the caregivers' capacity to soothe them, difficulties regulating emotion and expectations that support will be unavailable might emerge.
The infant's responses may, in turn, influence subsequent caregiving, improving or reinforcing these patterns.
As previously proposed, early impulsivity may be a partly distinct vulnerability in a substantial subset of individuals who later develop BPD.
These exchanges occur within broader family and ecological conditions that may support or constrain caregivers' capacity to respond.

Also, plasticity factors, as conceptualized in differential susceptibility theory, could interact with these varied nurturing or adverse environmental conditions and, alongside risk and protective factors, further increase the complexity of the possible developmental outcomes.

During early childhood, emotion regulation may become increasingly connected with expectations about others' availability, the ability to identify and communicate emotional states, and increasingly differentiated representations of self and others.
Under adverse circumstances, difficulties in these processes may play a role in the development of BPD or borderline personality organization.
Earlier relational patterns may increasingly shape self-appraisal.
In the absence of responsive support, children may come to regard their emotional needs as illegitimate or difficulties obtaining comfort as evidence that they are bad or unacceptable.
Conversely, with responsive support, emotional understanding and confidence in seeking help might develop.
The development of the sense of agency might also be influenced by such experiences.

The capacity to integrate contrasting experiences may help children maintain a sense of self and of being valued during conflict and accept contrasting impressions of another person as both caring and capable of causing disappointment.
Otherwise, their experience of themselves and others may be strongly influenced by the emotional quality of an exchange.
As peer and school relationships become increasingly important, these developing patterns may acquire new implications.

Anticipation of rejection may heighten emotional reactions to ambiguous social situations; intense distress may, in turn, impair interpretation of others' intentions, encourage withdrawal or urgent reassurance-seeking, and influence subsequent interpersonal responses.
Attempts to secure closeness or protect against anticipated rejection may inadvertently strain relationships, making the support sought less available and reinforcing expectations of exclusion.
Such exchanges may form vicious cycles in which interpersonal insecurity and emotional instability amplify one another.

Repeated activation of biological systems involved in stress responses during these exchanges may also shape subsequent stress reactivity and recovery, potentially contributing to the persistence of these cycles.
Experiences of acceptance and successful relational repair after conflict may interrupt these cycles and create opportunities to revise expectations of rejection.
Later on, during adolescence, increasing autonomy, closer relationships, and identity development may further alter the significance of these interconnected difficulties.

Pubertal changes and the continuing maturation of systems involved in stress responses, reward processing, and behavioral control may interact with these earlier vulnerabilities in the context of new developmental demands.
In some individuals, perceived separation or rejection may increasingly destabilize both their sense of self and their emotional state.

In some circumstances, close relationships may come to feel essential for maintaining self-worth, while difficulties sustaining a coherent sense of oneself and a sense of meaning and connection in one's life may lead to chronic feelings of emptiness.
Shame and rumination may also play a part, further amplifying distress and contributing to behaviors that only provide short-term relief but may maintain difficulties over time.
Impulsive responses may bring additional conflict or loss, reinforcing interpersonal insecurity and negative self-appraisals.
Borderline-related features may become recognizable during childhood and, in some individuals, develop into clinically significant borderline pathology during adolescence.
Their convergence may consolidate a pattern of affective, interpersonal, and identity instability, although its expression and severity vary across individuals.
Responses that may initially have been adaptive under negative circumstances might persist after those circumstances change, eventually losing their adaptive value and becoming detrimental.
This possible progression is neither necessary nor uniform.

The proposed course links early vulnerabilities with the emergence of mutually reinforcing difficulties in emotion regulation, relationships, and self-experience that may come to resemble a borderline pattern.
Similar vulnerabilities may be associated with different outcomes, while distinct combinations of experiences and developing capacities may contribute to borderline pathology.

Supportive relationships and changing contexts may facilitate new regulatory capacities, interpretations, and adaptations; however, an individual's ability to benefit from these opportunities might vary.
Findings consistent with differential susceptibility in borderline symptom development require further replication.
Whether particular combinations, sequences, or reciprocal effects distinguish borderline trajectories from other forms of psychopathology remains an empirical question.
Figures 2 and 3 illustrate selected proposed pathways exemplifying equifinality and multifinality, respectively, while Figure 4 provides a schematic overview of the proposed developmental framework.

text.text: Building on these possible developmental pathways, the priority is not simply to expand the list of potential etiological factors, but to clarify how previously identified vulnerabilities, experiences, and protective processes work together over time.
The framework organizes candidate developmental relationships rather than specifying a single causal model.
Its empirical value depends on whether these relationships improve explanation or prediction beyond simpler accounts.
A central question is why shared vulnerabilities lead to BPD rather than another disorder or sustained adaptation.

For example, prospective research has identified partly distinct predictors of borderline, depressive, and conduct symptoms [175], without establishing causal pathways or distinguishing new onset from persistence of earlier borderline features.
text.formatted: For example, prospective research has identified partly distinct predictors of borderline, depressive, and conduct symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b174">[175]</ref>, without establishing causal pathways or distinguishing new onset from persistence of earlier borderline features.

text.text: Building on this work, longitudinal studies following children into adulthood could examine how factors such as emotional vulnerability, poor behavioral control, and recurrent interpersonal difficulties combine and influence one another over time and whether these combinations are more strongly associated with later borderline pathology than with other outcomes.
These studies should account for prior symptoms and comorbidity and include comparisons with other psychiatric and personality disorders and sustained adaptation in relationships and everyday life.
A second proposition concerns the temporal relations among perceived interpersonal rejection, self-evaluation, and affect, and whether they differ between BPD and other disorders.
In experience sampling, arousal predicted subsequent perceived rejection without significant group differences [200].
text.formatted: In experience sampling, arousal predicted subsequent perceived rejection without significant group differences <ref type="bibr" target="#b199">[200]</ref>.

text.text: Self-esteem instability was greater in BPD than in anxiety disorders, whereas no significant difference in affective instability was detected [191].
text.formatted: Self-esteem instability was greater in BPD than in anxiety disorders, whereas no significant difference in affective instability was detected <ref type="bibr" target="#b190">[191]</ref>.

text.text: Related research found that higher negative affective arousal preceded lower self-esteem in BPD [215].
text.formatted: Related research found that higher negative affective arousal preceded lower self-esteem in BPD <ref type="bibr" target="#b214">[215]</ref>.

text.text: Although these findings do not establish a single sequence or a developmental pathway, studies combining intensive repeated assessments with longer-term follow-up could test competing temporal directions among these processes and whether the resulting patterns predict later borderline features more strongly than other psychiatric outcomes, after accounting for earlier symptoms.
Assessments should distinguish interpersonal events from perceived rejection, changes in self-esteem from broader identity disturbance, and short-term fluctuations from developmental change.
Developmental transactions provide a third focus.
Longitudinal findings on reciprocal parenting-child associations are mixed, with some prospective associations supported but not consistently across successive assessments [31, 216].
text.formatted: Longitudinal findings on reciprocal parenting-child associations are mixed, with some prospective associations supported but not consistently across successive assessments <ref type="bibr">[31,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b215">216]</ref>.

text.text: Observational research also links less mutual reinforcement of positive emotion during caregiver-child conflict with later borderline symptoms [217].
text.formatted: Observational research also links less mutual reinforcement of positive emotion during caregiver-child conflict with later borderline symptoms <ref type="bibr" target="#b216">[217]</ref>.

text.text: Repeated, multi-informant observations of conflict and repair could test whether failures to restore supportive interaction following distress predict poorer self-regulation and lower expectations of support and whether children's difficulties regulating emotion and behavior, in turn, predict changes in caregivers' responses.
Models should compare reciprocal pathways with child-driven, caregiver-driven, and shared-liability explanations, using family and genetic information where available.
Repeated biological measurements could examine whether changes in stress regulation precede or follow these transactions, without assuming mediation.
Protective pathways should be examined within the same developmental framework.
Existing findings identify candidate protective processes but leave their causal roles unresolved [128, 129].
text.formatted: Existing findings identify candidate protective processes but leave their causal roles unresolved <ref type="bibr" target="#b127">[128,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b128">129]</ref>.

text.text: Prospective studies could test whether reliable support predicts better functioning and fewer borderline features following adversity, and whether this association depends on the developing capacity to seek and use support.
Access, perceived availability, and actual use should be distinguished.

Differential susceptibility requires evidence that the same measured characteristic predicts greater responsiveness to both adverse and supportive conditions, rather than vulnerability to adversity alone.
Epigenetic research could examine whether DNA methylation changes help explain how biological vulnerability and experience jointly shape developmental outcomes.

Building on studies tracking DNA methylation during treatment [101] [102] [103], repeated assessments of methylation, adversity, support, stress regulation, and borderline features, beginning before disorder onset, could test whether methylation changes precede or follow emerging difficulties.

text.text: Comparisons among similarly exposed individuals developing BPD, other disorders, or sustained adaptation would address specificity.

Analyses should account for genetic influences, blood-cell composition, smoking, medication, and age, with adjustment guided by their timing and role in the proposed pathway, without assuming that peripheral methylation reflects brain processes.

Studies should compare competing explanations -adversity preceding methylation changes that predict later symptoms, symptoms preceding methylation changes, or shared influences contributing to both methylation changes and symptoms -while accounting for prior methylation and symptom levels.

Candidate mechanisms would require independent replication and experiments modifying implicated methylation in relevant cellular models to test effects on gene expression or stress-related cellular responses.

Across these research questions and proposed hypotheses, studies should distinguish categorical BPD, dimensional borderline features, general personality dysfunction, and borderline personality organization.
Repeated assessments should separate onset, persistence, and recovery, and within-person change from stable individual differences.

Long-term follow-up indicates that sustained symptomatic remission is more common than recovery encompassing good social and vocational functioning, highlighting the importance of assessing symptoms and functioning separately [218].
text.formatted: Long-term follow-up indicates that sustained symptomatic remission is more common than recovery encompassing good social and vocational functioning, highlighting the importance of assessing symptoms and functioning separately <ref type="bibr" target="#b217">[218]</ref>.

text.text: Confirmatory tests should prespecify the population, developmental period, measures, temporal sequence, competing models, and findings that would count against the hypothesis.
Replicated evidence favoring unidirectional or shared-liability explanations would challenge the corresponding reciprocal account.
Failure to predict borderline outcomes better than comparison outcomes would weaken claims of preferential prediction of BPD.
Responsiveness to adversity without greater responsiveness to support would not support differential susceptibility.
Such findings should narrow or revise the relevant hypotheses.
Interpretation requires sufficiently precise estimates and appropriate measurement timescales; nonsignificance alone is not decisive.

Building on existing treatment-process research (e.g., [219]), intervention studies could use targeted interventions and randomized comparisons where feasible to test whether changes in candidate processes precede improvements in downstream processes, symptoms, and functioning, although improvement alone would not establish developmental etiology.

text.text: BPD can be understood within a developmental framework as arising from the convergence of biological, psychological, and social processes.
Genetic, neurobiological, neuroendocrine, neurochemical, inflammatory, oxidative, and epigenetic processes may interact with adverse environments and psychological vulnerabilities.
This review integrates existing perspectives to clarify how these relationships may contribute to divergent outcomes, including borderline pathology, other disorders, and sustained adaptation.

The value of this integrative framework lies in organising multiple, partially competing theories and formulating testable developmental propositions while distinguishing supported findings from theoretical interpretations.
This review has several limitations.
As a narrative synthesis, it does not establish exhaustive coverage of the relevant literature.
The selection and interpretation of the literature may be subject to bias, while differences in study methods, populations, and definitions of borderline pathology limit comparability.
Integrating theories with differing assumptions and levels of empirical support also requires interpretive judgments.
The proposed synthesis should therefore be regarded as provisional rather than as a validated etiological model.
Future research should clarify how vulnerabilities, experiences, and protective processes work together over time to shape different developmental outcomes.

Clinically, this perspective encourages individualized formulation that considers how vulnerabilities, current difficulties, and available supports interact, helping identify priorities for treatment.
Diagnostic classification should support this formulation and guide care responsive to the person's difficulties and goals. and developed the figures and supplementary materials.
